New Delhi [India], October 15 (ANI): The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will come into force on October 20, while India and Canada are targeting the conclusion of negotiations for their proposed trade agreement by the end of 2026, as India seeks to expand market access for exporters amid global trade uncertainties.
According to a presentation by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday, India and Canada are aiming to conclude negotiations for their proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) by the end of 2026.
The fifth round of negotiations between the two countries was held in Ottawa from October 5 to 9, with discussions covering market access for goods and services, investment, rules of origin, intellectual property rights and trade remedies. The next round of talks is planned for early November in New Delhi.
The proposed agreement is expected to strengthen economic ties between the two countries by reducing trade barriers and improving market access for businesses.
Meanwhile, the India-New Zealand FTA, signed in April 2026, will become operational on October 20. The agreement will provide duty-free access to Indian exports entering New Zealand, creating opportunities for sectors such as textiles, leather, footwear, engineering goods and processed agricultural products.
These developments come as India's merchandise exports have recorded growth across several major trading partners during the first half of the current financial year.
According to the Commerce Ministry's trade data, India's exports to the United Kingdom increased to USD 7.32 billion during April-September 2026, from USD 6.83 billion a year earlier. The India-UK trade agreement came into force in July this year.
Exports to China also rose to USD 11.41 billion from USD 8.39 billion, while shipments to the European Union increased to USD 31.92 billion from USD 30.61 billion.
India has earlier concluded FTA negotiations with the European Union, although the agreement is yet to enter into force.
The ministry's presentation further showed that negotiations are underway with several other trading partners, including the United States, Israel, Chile and Peru.
India is also pursuing reviews or upgrades of existing trade agreements with Australia, ASEAN, South Korea and Sri Lanka.
The ongoing negotiations and implementation of new agreements are part of India's efforts to diversify export destinations and secure better market access for domestic businesses amid changing global tariff policies. (ANI)

articles.title: Explained | UK universities withdrawing admissions offered to Indian, Pakistani applicants amid stricter visa rules; what you need to know - Deccan Herald
articles.summary: Explained | UK universities withdrawing admissions offered to Indian, Pakistani applicants amid stricter visa rules; what you need to know  Deccan HeraldUK universities withdraw admission offers to Nigerian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi students over fears of losing sponsorship licences  Business Insider AfricaUK visa rules cause decline in foreign students from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nigeria  The Indian ExpressUK universities withdraw international student of...
articles.full_text:
Universities in the United Kingdom (UK) are withdrawing admission offers to some international students as the government tightens student visa rules, according to a Financial Times report.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
The trend has reportedly affected students from countries including Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nigeria and India.
What has changed in the UK’s visa rules?
This year, the UK government introduced a stricter Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) framework for institutions sponsoring international students from June 1, 2026.
Under the revised rules, universities must keep their student visa refusal rate below 5 per cent, down from the earlier limit of 10 per cent. They must also ensure that at least 95 per cent of sponsored students enrol in their courses, up from 90 per cent earlier. The course completion requirement remains 85 per cent for assessments from June 2026 and will rise to 90 per cent from June 2027, according to the UK Home Office.
The government introduced the changes to strengthen oversight of student recruitment and address concerns about visa misuse and students failing to enrol or complete their courses.
Why are universities withdrawing offers?
The stricter rules have raised concerns among universities that a high visa refusal rate could affect their ability to recruit international students.
According to the Financial Times, some universities have started withdrawing admission offers before students receive visa decisions to avoid refusals that could push their rates above the permitted limit.
Under the UK Home Office rules, applications are not counted as refusals if a university withdraws the student's Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) before a visa decision is made.
A CAS is the sponsorship reference a licensed institution assigns to a student to support their UK Student visa application. An admission offer alone does not guarantee a visa.
However, universities that fail to meet the new requirements do not automatically lose their licences.
The UK Home Office uses a red-amber-green rating system to assess their compliance. A red rating can lead to an action plan and restrictions on the number of CAS references a university can issue. Serious or repeated violations can result in the loss of its licence to sponsor international students.
How are Indian students affected?
According to the Home Office data, 10.5 per cent of UK study visa applications were withdrawn in January-June 2026, compared with 2.3 per cent in the same period in 2025 and 0.4 per cent in 2023.
Pakistan recorded the highest reported withdrawal rate among the nationalities highlighted, at 40.9 per cent in January-June 2026, compared with 3 per cent a year earlier. The rate rose to 23.5 per cent for Bangladesh and 22.7 per cent for Nigeria.
For Indian applicants, the reported rate increased from 1.2 per cent in the first half of 2025 to 5.2 per cent in the same period this year.
These figures refer to withdrawn visa applications, not visa refusals or withdrawn admission offers. The figures indicate that Indian applicants are also affected by the changing environment, although the reported withdrawal rate was substantially higher for Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Nigerian applicants.
The revised compliance framework does not impose a blanket restriction on Indian students. However, the data suggests that some universities are taking a more cautious approach to international recruitment because of the potential consequences of visa refusals.

New Delhi [India], October 15 (ANI): India's merchandise exports to the United States rose 11.1 per cent to USD 50.81 billion during April-September 2026, despite tariff-related disruptions, while imports from the US increased by 26 per cent, according to data presented by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday.
Exports to the US increased from USD 45.73 billion in the corresponding period last year, while imports rose to USD 32.33 billion from USD 25.66 billion.
The figures show that bilateral trade continued to expand despite tariff uncertainties, although India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to USD 18.48 billion from USD 20.07 billion a year earlier.
The US remained India's largest merchandise export destination during the first half of the current financial year.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations for the proposed India-US trade agreement were progressing in the right direction, with both countries working towards concluding the deal at the earliest.
'The negotiations are in the right direction. Probably, we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing it at the earliest possible time,' Agrawal said during a press briefing.
He explained that the agreement would depend on the finalisation of the broader tariff framework in the United States, where a parallel process is underway under Section 301.
'The deal has to be signed when the overall tariff structure is getting formalised. There is parallel work being done in the US also to get back the tariff structure based on some of the outcomes of the 301,' he said.
Agrawal further emphasised that India was seeking preferential access to the American market to ensure its exporters could compete effectively with other countries.
'When you do a trade deal, it gives you not only market access in each other's markets; it gives you preferential market access in a particular market,' he said.
He added that India's preferential market access relative to its competitors would form part of the new tariff framework.
The ongoing negotiations are significant as both countries seek to strengthen bilateral trade ties while addressing tariff-related challenges affecting market access. (ANI)

articles.title: India's rice export earnings rise 12.9% in April-August; BIRC to focus on policy, incentives - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India's rice export earnings rise 12.9% in April-August; BIRC to focus on policy, incentives  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
India's rice export earnings rose 12.9 per cent to ₹45,739 crore during April-August 2026, with stable trade policies, accessible incentives and better market access needed to sustain the growth, according to the Indian Rice Exporters' Federation (IREF).
Basmati rice exports contributed ₹22,864 crore, up 11.6 per cent, while non-Basmati exports reached ₹22,874 crore, registering growth of 14.2 per cent over April-August 2025, the federation said in a release. The figures reflect growth in export value in rupee terms rather than physical shipment volumes.
Against this backdrop, the Bharat International Rice Conference (BIRC) 2026, scheduled for October 23-25 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, will examine trade policies, export incentives and opportunities to expand India's presence in international markets.
Dev Garg, National Vice President of IREF, stressed the need to translate policy announcements into benefits exporters can access. "An incentive matters to an exporter only when it can be accessed, claimed and translated into a real business benefit. Likewise, a trade agreement creates an opportunity only when the exporter understands whether their product qualifies," Garg said. "At BIRC 2026, we want to close that gap between policy announcements and practical results-helping businesses enter new markets, manage costs and build dependable export relationships."
Bipin Aggarwal, Vice President (Kakinada), IREF, and Director of Andhra Pradesh-based rice exporter CLRK, said policy consistency and timely incentives were crucial for non-Basmati exporters. "Our industry works on tight margins, and changes in export regulations, freight costs or import duties can directly affect our ability to secure international orders," he said.
"We need a policy framework that supports long-term export commitments, simplifies access to incentives and helps Indian rice compete in price-sensitive markets across Africa and Asia."
Meanwhile, IREF said substantial rice reserves were likely to cushion exports against a projected decline in production.
Citing the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), the release said India's rice production is projected to fall from approximately 154 million tonnes in 2025-26 to 147 million tonnes in 2026-27 amid adverse weather conditions. Government rice stocks have been reported above 38 million tonnes, nearly four times the prescribed October buffer norm of 10.25 million tonnes, according to the release.
IREF expects reserves to remain comfortably above buffer requirements even with a reduction in stocks, supporting domestic food security and export supplies. The conference session will also examine export credit, insurance, guarantees and warehouse-receipt financing.
A proposed "BIRC 2026 Rice Export Policy Watch" will identify five major policy developments that could influence India's rice trade over the next 12 months, distinguishing between measures already in force, announced changes, proposed reforms and trade agreements under negotiation.
IREF said policy stability and accessible incentives would be critical to diversifying export markets, strengthening India's presence in Africa, Europe and Asia, and encouraging investment in processing, quality improvement and value-added products.

articles.title: Indias Free Trade Agreements Could Boost GDP By $170 Billion By 2035 - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: Indias Free Trade Agreements Could Boost GDP By $170 Billion By 2035  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
India's expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could increase its gross domestic product (GDP) by $140 billion to $170 billion by 2035, according to a Bloomberg Economics report.
The report suggested that stronger trade partnerships could help India withstand higher American tariffs while encouraging exports, foreign investment and productivity growth.
Existing agreements are projected to raise GDP by 1.2% above the baseline by 2035.
Implementation of agreements with the European Union (EU) and New Zealand from 2027 could increase the gain to 1.7%, equivalent to approximately $140 billion at constant 2025 dollar values.
FTAs Could Lift GDP By 2.1%
Bloomberg Economics estimated that a trade agreement with the US could contribute another 0.2 percentage points to India's GDP.
Successful negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel could add a further 0.2 percentage points.
Together, these developments could lift economic output by 2.1%, or approximately $170 billion, by 2035.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal recently said India was negotiating agreements with eight to nine additional countries or groups representing approximately $15 trillion in combined GDP.
He said India had concluded nine FTAs covering 38 developed countries and economies worth $60 trillion over the previous four-and-a-half years.
The report projected trade volumes, including imports, could increase approximately 10% by 2035 compared with 2024.
US Tariffs May Have Limited Impact
Bloomberg Economics estimated that average US tariffs on Indian goods had increased from 2.4% in 2024 to 11.6%.
Although these duties could reduce Indian merchandise exports to America by approximately 20% by 2035, the report anticipated a negligible overall GDP impact.
It noted that less than 2% of India's economic output depended on US markets.
India's GDP growth was projected at 6.9% in 2026 and 7.4% in 2027, while inflation could reach 4.5% and 5.3%, respectively.
The report forecast the repo rate at 5.50% in 2026 and 5.75% in 2027.
It also estimated that artificial intelligence (AI) could increase annual GDP growth by 0.4 to 0.9 percentage points through productivity improvements, despite increasingly concentrated global capital flows.

articles.full_text:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Can India's latest FTAs put it on the road to Viksit Atmanirbhar Bharat?
Can India's latest FTAs put it on the road to Viksit Atmanirbhar Bharat?
India's FTAs can boost export-led growth, but sustainable gains will depend on responsible subsidies, stronger labour standards and environment-friendly production
premium
A cargo ship at port highlights India’s growing role in global trade and its push to expand export markets through free trade agreements
India, a country known to have been reticent in liberalising trade till very recently, has negotiated around nine agreements between 2021 and 2026. The free trade agreement (FTA) partners span around 38 developed countries and, as per latest reports, India is negotiating with eight to nine blocs and individual countries to collectively account for 75 per cent of global trade.
For a country branded a “tariff king” by US President Donald Trump, and perceived as obstructionist at the World Trade Organization, India seems to be redrawing its earlier perceptions in the world over the last 5 years.
India’s recent surge in signing FTAs seems to be the result of a number of developments. Tackling China in competition in domestic markets is near-impossible (despite lower labour costs) without increasing sales volumes in the markets abroad which, in turn, help build scale economies, reducing production costs. Additionally, the recent Trump tariffs, broadly impacting all economies of the world, have pushed most countries to reach trade deals at an unprecedented rate, reflecting a collective commitment to free trade.
Indian FTAs span countries which are developed markets, including the European Union (EU), European Free Trade Association (Efta), and Australia, as well as countries which are home to a significant portion of the Indian diaspora. These include the United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates and Oman. Finally, negotiations are in progress with countries which would help secure India’s supply chain of critical rare earth elements. Peru and Chile fall under this category. India’s earlier comprehensive agreements with Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia have their own role in comprehensive cooperation on multiple fronts. The India-EU trade deal, branded as the “mother of all trade deals”, is creating a positive outlook for future growth in external demand-driven economic growth. However, do the FTAs have implications for India’s vision of becoming atmanirbhar and, finally, viksit?
In a world where the US turns protectionist and large corporates strategise, keeping tensions with China in mind, the FTAs provide an opportunity for Indian businesses and the Indian government to prioritise some changes and avoid some others to enable longer term sustainability of India’s position in global markets as well as catapult India to a Viksit Bharat.
A quick look at the pain points for globalisation, emerging from the stalemate at the WTO, the experience of mega-regional agreements, and current reactions from the US could help draw some quick lessons on how India could use this opportunity to make the best of the world’s China+1 strategy.
Production subsidies and dumping
In the last couple of decades, one observes the repeated use of anti-dumping cases against countries like China at the WTO. State-sponsored unfair subsidies in China helped reap cost advantages beyond the scale economies of operations. Most Chinese products thus got cheaper than those of China’s counterparts across the world. While the Chinese labour costs were lower, the greater scale of operations, further facilitated by state subsidies on a massive scale, have adversely impacted most countries, especially the developed West. Advantages in production costs due to lower labour costs should be fair, providing some breathing space for production by other countries. While India prioritises growth through production linked incentives (PLIs), a sunset clause linked to growth in the scale of operations or transitioning to research and development (R&D)-linked subsidies is ideal for sustained export-led growth.
Environment
The developed world is concerned about environmental standards and protection of marine life. The WTO agreement on fisheries subsidies, reached in 2022, and the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) of the EU are worth our attention. The EU tries to protect the environment and tax non-environment-friendly methods of production. The India-EU FTA does not make any carve-outs on the applicability of the CBAM. In essence, India faces the TBT (technical barriers to trade) on similar levels as other countries. Adoption of environment-friendly production techniques by Indian businesses would help both in achieving greater market access in any developed country and in moving towards a truly Viksit Bharat.
Forced labour
The US has imposed additional tariffs for the use of forced labour or labour-unfriendly work conditions against selected countries, including India through the forced-labour Section 301 tariffs. These tariffs are a result of the US’s failure to block labour-unfriendly products entering the US markets from countries like China. Going back to 2013, India’s use of child labour for manufacturing rugby balls for Summit Sports in Australia drew enough negative media attention internationally. While the WTO has never acted to ensure quality work standards for workers involved in producing tradable goods, the International Labour Organization (ILO) standards would be ideal. Once again moving towards viable labour standards, including appropriate overtime pay, would create the base for a Viksit Bharat and avoid future possibilities of tariffs on grounds of forced labour.
Tariff-jumping transhipment
Rules of origin violations (to bypass tariffs) have been highlighted by the US recently. India earlier raised similar issues with regard to China, leading to a review of the India-Asean (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) agreement. Contrary to China’s conditions, India signing FTAs with most countries would allow it market access at lower tariff rates and the need to bypass tariffs should not arise. India should avoid using FTAs to push its products to non-FTA countries.
It may be prudent to note that mega-regional agreements like the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) have very different stands on each of the four areas mentioned above. While the CPTPP commits to environment-friendly production, protection of labour standards and avoiding state-sponsored production subsidies, the China-led RCEP is nearly silent on all of these. It is easy to see that relaxed labour and environment standards along with state subsidies are the building blocks of sustained trade advantage for nations like China and Vietnam. The developed West sees these as unfair to their own workers/citizens as jobs are lost along with environmental degradation in exchange for cheaper imported products.
Learning from the above, India has the choice to: a) craft its subsidies with appropriate sunset clauses, b) protect labour standards, and c) adopt environment-friendly production to sustainably position itself in global markets. This would be the basis of a truly Viksit Bharat.
The writer is associate professor of economics at the Indian Institutes of Management (IIM) Nagpur

articles.title: IPS calls for investment- and export-led growth to sustain Sri Lanka’s recovery - Hiru News
articles.summary: IPS calls for investment- and export-led growth to sustain Sri Lanka’s recovery  Hiru News
articles.full_text:
Sri Lanka must move away from debt-financed spending, tax concessions and import-intensive consumption to sustain its economic recovery, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) has said, calling for a growth strategy centred on private investment, productivity and competitive exports.
In its newly released Sri Lanka: State of the Economy 2026 report, titled Policy Choices for Durable Growth, the IPS said the country’s next challenge was to accelerate economic growth without reopening the fiscal and external vulnerabilities that contributed to the 2022 economic crisis.
With limited fiscal and external space, the next phase of expansion must depend on stronger investment, a more competitive and diversified export sector, and the creation of better-quality jobs, the institute said.
“Sri Lanka can no longer rely on debt-financed spending, tax concessions or import-intensive consumption as drivers of growth,” the IPS said in a statement announcing the report.
The assessment comes as the economy continues to recover from the crisis. Real GDP grew by 5% in both 2024 and 2025, and by 4.7% in the first half of 2026, according to the release.
Inflation has eased considerably from its 2022 peak, progress has been made in external debt restructuring, and foreign reserves have been rebuilt to more comfortable levels, the institute said.
However, sustaining these gains will require a growth model that can withstand future shocks while delivering broad-based improvements in living standards.
The report calls for continued macroeconomic stability alongside measures to improve productivity and ensure more effective use of scarce public resources.
“The challenge then is to accelerate growth without reopening the fiscal and external vulnerabilities that contributed to the crisis,” the release said.
Human capital development and labour market reforms are also identified as central to the next phase of growth. The IPS highlighted the need to address skills gaps, create better-quality employment and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
With around two-thirds of Sri Lanka’s workers employed informally, the report identifies improved labour market outcomes and stronger social protection as priorities for ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are more widely shared.
The institute said better-quality employment and a workforce equipped with relevant skills would be essential to improving productivity and enabling more people to participate in and benefit from economic expansion.
Building resilience to climate-related disruptions, energy shocks and external pressures is another key requirement for sustained economic progress.
Recent climate-related disruptions and global energy shocks have demonstrated the importance of placing resilience at the centre of Sri Lanka’s development strategy, the IPS said.
Investment in renewable energy, food systems, infrastructure and disaster preparedness could help protect future growth while reducing the economy’s exposure to shocks.
The report also examines how infrastructure investment, regional development and responses to changing population dynamics could contribute to more inclusive growth.
Its policy recommendations cover trade, fiscal management, labour markets, urbanisation, energy, agriculture, social protection and human capital development.
The IPS said Sri Lanka could achieve its long-term development ambitions through reforms that strengthen competitiveness and resilience while ensuring the benefits of economic progress are broadly shared.

articles.summary: First China-Pakistan army joint training features an all-Chinese equipment lineup, signaling deep interoperability: expert  Global TimesChina, Pakistan hold first joint army drills in Xinjiang with all-Chinese weapons  Telegraph IndiaChina, Pakistan hold high-altitude army drills with Beijing-supplied arms  The Times of IndiaPakistani, Chinese armies begin joint training exercise in Xinjiang  DawnHow China-Pakistan’s Xinjiang war games affect India &n...
articles.full_text:
Image of the opening ceremony of the China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training held at a training base in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Photo: Screenshot from the CCTV's military channel
The first China-Pakistan army joint training Karakoram 2026 kicked off on Wednesday, with all weapons and equipment provided by the Chinese side, China Central Television's (CCTV) military channel reported. A military affairs expert said the choice of medium-weight wheeled vehicles for high-altitude operations, and Pakistan's use of an all-Chinese lineup, signal deepening military trust and potential future procurement.
The opening ceremony for the China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training was held at a training base in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. It is the first army joint training between the two countries, themed on joint counter-terrorism and clearance operations in high-altitude areas, said the report.
The report said that all weapons and equipment in the training were provided by China, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as artillery, unmanned and anti-unmanned systems.
Wang Yunfei, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the two types of vehicles are both wheeled platforms. In high-altitude areas, wheeled armored vehicles have their own advantages. Unlike tracked vehicles, they are faster, especially during road maneuvers, and easier to maintain, making them well-suited for movement and combat missions on the plateau.
The all-Chinese equipment lineup covers multiple categories and forms a relatively complete combat system, he said. On one hand, it shows China has provided weapons and equipment technology to Pakistan.
On the other hand, these weapons could be procured by Pakistan in future military trade, further expanding the presence of Chinese equipment in the Pakistan Army. This joint training thus serves as a rehearsal and a process of familiarization.
From a broader perspective, it also reflects strategic mutual trust, showing that military cooperation between the two countries has reached a high level. Building this kind of deep interoperability will lay a solid foundation for future joint operations between the two armies in counter-terrorism, border control and other areas, the expert said.
Zhang Jueshe, another military affairs expert, told the Global Times that China and Pakistan complement each other well in the field of counter-terrorism, while cooperation can be advanced via intelligence sharing, joint operations, technology transfers, experience exchanges and economic cooperation.
"China could provide Pakistan with technical and equipment support, including drones and smart combat platforms, to boost its surveillance and early warning capacity against terrorist groups, and also conduct experience training," he noted.
Pakistan's experience in addressing complex border security situations, handling local separatist forces and coordinating counter-terrorism efforts can also provide references for China to tackle similar non-traditional security challenges, Zhang added.
On Saturday, Senior Colonel Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of National Defense, announced that in mid- and late October, Chinese and Pakistani armies will hold Karakoram 2026 joint army training in Korla, Xinjiang. Focusing on joint counter-terrorism operations in high-altitude areas, the activity will include skills training in UAV operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and cover joint command and live-force exercises.
The exercise will expand the scope of China-Pakistan military cooperation, reflect growing mutual trust, and strengthen counter-terrorism collaboration through the sharing of experience and expertise, Zhang said.

articles.title: NTPC in talks with Japan, South Korea, Germany for green fuel exports - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: NTPC in talks with Japan, South Korea, Germany for green fuel exports  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
NTPC is currently engaged in discussions with potential buyers from Japan, South Korea, and Germany. The company aims to establish a green hydrogen hub in Andhra Pradesh for producing green ammonia and methanol.
India's top power producer NTPC is in talks with potential buyers in Japan, South Korea and Germany for green ammonia and other low-carbon fuels, Chairman Gurdeep Singh said on Tuesday.
India has outlined plans to become a major green hydrogen producer, even as developers worldwide have struggled to secure the long-term offtake agreements required to underpin large-scale investments.
NTPC is in talks with prospective overseas customers as it develops a proposed green hydrogen hub in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh, Singh said at an event organised by the Indian Chamber of Commerce.

articles.full_text:
• Economic instability erodes household purchasing power; heavy rains, floods trigger acute crop losses
• South Asia remains in the ‘serious’ category; global hunger rises after two decades
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia on the 2026 Global Hunger Index released on Wednesday, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks and global conflicts.
Published jointly by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and the Swiss organisation Helvetas under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, the report reveals that progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018.
In Pakistan, economic instability and sharp food price inflation have eroded households’ purchasing power and constrained access to food. Undernourishment in the country has climbed from low in 2018 to medium, while child wasting has risen toward the high threshold.
Across South Asia, the situation remains serious with a regional score of 23.5. Although the region’s score has fallen substantially from an alarming 37.5 in 2000, most of that progress occurred before 2018.
While Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved from the alarming to the serious category since 2000, child stunting remains very high.
Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall, whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. Child mortality rates in both nations have declined from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels today.
The report warned that high levels of acute food insecurity will persist across the region. Heavy rains and flooding caused localised crop losses in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures negatively affected Afghanistan’s 2026 cereal-growing season.
According to Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates, 218 million people in South Asia, including Iran, were undernourished between 2023 and 2025, representing roughly one-third of the global total.
Globally, hunger is rising again after nearly two decades of progress. The 2026 global score stands at 18.1, worsening from 17.6 in 2018.
Hunger has increased in 32 countries since 2018, and 57 countries are on track to miss achieving even low hunger levels by 2030.
Three of the index’s four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — have worsened, while only child mortality has continued to decline slightly.
State-based armed conflicts, now at their highest level since World War II, alongside frequent extreme weather events, are major drivers of this reversal.
The war in Iran and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are driving up fuel, transportation and fertiliser costs.
Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea export restrictions threaten higher wheat prices, making basic supplies unaffordable in the Global South.
Compounding the crisis, international spending on food security has fallen to 2016-2017 levels, forcing cuts to aid programmes and emergency rations. The report urged governments to reverse funding cuts for humanitarian assistance and data collection to prevent and manage future crises.

Yemen's Houthis are seeking Chinese parts for advanced ballistic missiles, raising concerns over regional security and the group's growing weapons capabilities.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are seeking Chinese-made components to develop an advanced ballistic missile system that could improve their ability to strike targets in Saudi Arabia and Israel, according to a new report by Conflict Armament Research (CAR).
The report, released on Wednesday, October 14, said two shipments containing suspected missile components had been intercepted by Yemeni authorities. The equipment originated in China and was intended for delivery to Hodeidah, a port in Yemen controlled by the Houthis, according to the Associated Press (AP).
Researchers said the parts could help the group build a missile similar to Iran's Kheibar Shekan, a precision-guided ballistic missile with a reported range of around 2,000 kilometres.
The findings suggest the Houthis may be developing a greater ability to assemble advanced weapons inside Yemen rather than relying only on complete weapons supplied from abroad.
Report details suspected Chinese components for Houthi missiles
According to CAR, the shipments contained several parts linked to missile production, including stabilising fin cores, rocket motor closures with nozzle attachments and rocket motor igniters. The cargo also included phenolic resin, a material used to make heat shields that protect missiles during flight through the atmosphere.
Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at CAR, said the findings pointed to a more ambitious weapons programme than previously understood.
“The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed,” Hinz said.
He added that the components were highly specialised and that making the missile would require design information.
“They're not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications,” Hinz said.
Also Read: Houthi strike hits building at Saudi Aramco headquarters
China responds as questions grow over missile supplies
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, did not directly address the report's findings. He said Beijing was meeting its international obligations and maintained that China carefully controls exports of military and dual-use goods.
“China has always adopted a prudent and responsible approach to the export of military products and strictly controls the export of dual-use items,” Chang said.
China has significant economic ties with both Saudi Arabia and Iran. It also helped broker a rapprochement between the two countries in 2023 and has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi airports.
The reported shipments could put further pressure on Beijing as tensions in the region continue to rise.
Also Read: How are Houthis able to penetrate Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Houthis expand weapons programme beyond Iranian supplies
The Houthis have developed more advanced weapons over the years, moving beyond older weapons seized from Yemen's military. They have used ballistic missiles and long-range drones in attacks on regional targets, including Israel.
Iran has been a key source of weapons designs and components for the group. However, analysts say the Houthis are increasingly seeking parts through wider international supply networks.
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the group was diversifying its sources of supply.
“Redundancy is an asset, not a liability in military planning,” he said. “With a blockade of Iran in place, the Houthis are diversifying.”
The Century Foundation, a US think tank, has also described the group's weapons supply chain as involving smugglers and businesses operating across several countries.
Advanced missiles could raise regional security concerns
The development could have wider consequences for the Gulf, where Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks. Analysts say access to more advanced missile components could improve the group's ability to assemble weapons and target distant locations.
Kristian Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at the Baker Institute, warned that the reported supply links could increase pressure on China from Saudi Arabia, its largest trading partner.
“Now that the situation has really escalated and seen these attacks on infrastructure and airports, we could see more pressure from the Saudis,” he said.
The full extent of the Houthis' ability to manufacture the reported missile system remains unclear.

India: Resilient real GDP growth amid rising inflation
Event
Against the odds, India’s real GDP growth has so far shown high resilience, comfortably remaining the fastest-growing G20 economy. In its latest forecasts, the IMF expects real GDP growth of 7% in the current financial year, FY2026/27 (ending in March 2027), and in FY2027/28, down from 7.8% in FY2025/26.
Impact
Over the past two years, India has been hit by the US trade war, a brief violent military conflict with Pakistan and the fallout from the Middle East conflict.
These three external shocks have harmed the economy through various transmission channels, particularly higher inflation, a widening current account deficit (largely due to costlier energy imports) and a weakening rupee, which has fallen to a historic low despite interventions by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
The most harmful impact comes from India’s high dependence on energy and fertiliser imports from the Gulf and its broad economic and financial links with the region.
Given its limited strategic oil reserves and heavy reliance on fuel imports, which account for close to one-third of total imports and come mainly from the Gulf, the authorities have adopted a mix of mitigating measures.
These include reducing energy demand, increasing fuel imports from alternative suppliers, especially Russia, and diversifying energy sources.
More recently, oil supplies to India have improved sharply as Gulf countries have used alternative, albeit costlier, trade routes.
Still, since June, Delhi has been unable to prevent inflation – which reached 5.
5% in September – from rising and fluctuating above the RBI’s 4% target as higher food and oil prices have spilled over into the wider economy.
The RBI therefore raised its policy rate to 5.
5% for the first time since early 2023, in line with the monetary tightening observed across advanced economies.

Despite these external shocks, the economy has managed to keep a strong momentum thanks to resilient household consumption, a large domestic market and a well-performing IT services sector. That said, higher inflation, less favourable financial market conditions and a poor monsoon, combined with El Niño, are expected to affect domestic demand and the economy over the next year. The geopolitical context continues to produce mixed outcomes. The US trade war has had only a moderate impact on India’s economy following the trade deal reached in February, which included much lower tariffs on a broad range of Indian exports. However, uncertainty persists as difficult negotiations continue against the backdrop of deteriorated bilateral relations. At the same time, India is benefiting from trade diversion and shifts in global supply chains, as shown by the surge in FDI in the pharmaceutical and electronics sectors, which is helping to offset the impact of the US trade war.
In the coming months, an extended Middle East conflict and oil price shock will represent the dominant downside risks to India’s economic outlook. For the time being, the short-term risk outlook is stable, with a short-term political risk rating in category 2/7, supported by robust foreign exchange reserves, and a business environment risk rating still in category E/G as the rupee remains under depreciation pressure, having fallen by 6% against the US dollar between January and mid-October, while inflation is rising and an economic slowdown is expected.

Print: 16 Oct 2026
The Great Redrawing
of Global Trade Maps
The surge in US tariffs since President Donald Trump
returned to the White House in January 2025 is redrawing global trade links.
After 19 months of wild swings, we estimate the average US tariff rate stood at
10.7% in August, up from 2.3% in 2024. 
That reflects sectoral tariffs—mainly on cars and metals,
and country-specific levies set at around 10%-12.5% under the Section 301
forced labor action. Tariffs at this rate could lower US goods imports by
roughly 15% compared with the previous regime. Threats and investigations point
to more hikes to come.
Other countries are responding by diversifying trade links
and accelerating negotiations with new partners. Since the start of 2025, the
European Union has signed new or updated agreements with Mercosur and Mexico
and concluded negotiations with Indonesia, India and Australia. 
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China signed
an upgraded free-trade agreement in October 2025. Canada signed several
agreements in 2025-26 and moved to launch, accelerate or revive others.
India is no exception. During 2025-26, agreements with the
European Free Trade Association, the UK and Oman entered into force, adding to
deals with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022. 
India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded
negotiations with the EU. In addition, New Delhi is pursuing other
partners—including the Eurasian Economic Union—and has sought an agreement with
the Gulf Cooperation Council.
At the same time, India has pursued deeper trade links with
the US since Trump and Narendra Modi announced plans for a bilateral agreement
in February 2025. The relationship has been rocky. In the second half of 2025,
India faced some of the highest additional tariffs among major US trading
partners after Washington imposed a 25% reciprocal tariff and an additional 25%
duty linked to Russian oil purchases.
Tensions have eased since then. While sectoral tariffs remain in place, the US removed the Russia-related 25% tariff and lowered reciprocal rates on India to 18% in February. In addition, under the Section 301 forced labor action, which has replaced reciprocal tariffs, India has been set a rate of 10%, lower than the 12.5% slapped on many other partners. This is paving the way for an interim deal, though reaching a more comprehensive agreement may prove difficult.
What Trade
Reshuffling Means for the Indian Economy
Using a computable general equilibrium model, we estimate
how India’s trade deals could reshape its economy over the next decade.
We start by assessing the impact of US tariffs at their
August level, relative to 2024 duties. We calculate that the average tariff on
Indian goods sold to the US has risen to 11.6%, from 2.4% in 2024. By 2035, we
estimate the tariffs will cut Indian goods exports to the US by about
one-fifth. But the hit to India’s economy should be limited. Less than 2% of
its output relies on US markets, and stronger exports elsewhere should cushion
the blow. We estimate the effect on gross domestic product will be negligible.
We then model the FTAs already concluded or under
negotiation through three channels:
First, we adjust bilateral tariffs using a stylized schedule
that captures the key elements of the deals. India’s partners eliminate all
tariffs on Indian goods in the first year. India eliminates tariffs on
industrial products and halves those on agricultural products, implementing
half of the reduction in the first year and the rest by year 10.
Second, building on Metivier et al. (2023), we assume the
cost of nontariff measures on goods and services falls gradually by 25% over 15
years, with an additional reduction in NTMs on services to capture lower uncertainty
from bilateral agreements.
Third, using Prasad et al. (2008), we add a productivity
boost from higher FDI in line with commitments under the deals: $100 billion
over 15 years for EFTA (roughly $35 billion of which is expected to be
additional), and $20 billion for New Zealand (almost all additional).
For US-India negotiations, we model an interim agreement
under which India grants the US roughly the same tariff reductions as under its
other deals. The US cuts sectoral duties on automotive products to 15%
(including most-favored-nation tariffs) but keeps the 50% metal tariffs and 10%
Section 301 duties on most covered products—similar to the conditions it
granted other deal partners such as the EU or Japan. We still expect the
agreement to reduce tensions and uncertainty and to deliver the same decline in
NTMs as India’s other FTAs.
Our analysis suggests FTAs already in force should raise
India’s GDP by 1.2% by 2035 relative to baseline, rising to 1.7% if the EU and
New Zealand agreements are implemented from 2027, a gain of about $140 billion
at constant 2025 US dollars. A US deal would add 0.2 percentage point. If
negotiations with the EAEU, GCC and Israel conclude over the next few years,
the gain could rise by another 0.2 ppt, leaving GDP 2.1% higher (about $170
billion) by 2035.
Trade volumes would rise even faster. By 2035, Indian exports could be almost 10% above baseline if all deals are implemented. Imports also would climb as households and businesses gain access to new products and services and manufacturers become more integrated into global value chains.
How Domestic Trends
Could Compound the Boost
Signing FTAs is only the first step. Reaping the full
benefits will require India to sustain its reform momentum. Effective
implementation; reliable access to energy, critical minerals and advanced
technologies; and unlocking the potential of India’s vast labor force will all
be important.
We model an upside scenario in which two domestic trends
amplify the gains:
Lower production costs. India has cut corporate taxes,
introduced subsidies, ramped up infrastructure investment to lower logistics
costs and funded incentives to boost workers’ skills. Regardless of trade
developments, some of these benefits likely have already materialized. In this
upside scenario we assume a further boost to manufacturers’ efficiency, which
we model as a roughly 2% decline in production costs. That could add roughly 1
ppt to export gains and 0.5 ppt to GDP gains by 2035.
Tap India’s agricultural labor potential. More than 40% of
Indian workers remain in agriculture—little changed over the past decade—with
high underemployment. By comparison, in rapidly industrializing Vietnam the
share has fallen from more than 40% to around 25%, while agricultural output
per worker has risen rapidly and now exceeds India’s by almost 60%. We model a
similar productivity boost in India phased in over a decade, allowing workers
to shift toward expanding manufacturing and services. This adds slightly more
than 1 ppt to export growth and about 2 ppts to GDP gains.
India is pairing an ambitious industrial strategy with an equally ambitious trade agenda. If it gets the combination right, it could become a powerful new engine of long-term growth. US tariffs are a drag. For India, and the world, the right response could yet deliver a development win.

IIT Kanpur and IIM Bangalore's NSRCEL have joined forces to support deep-tech startups, strengthening India's innovation ecosystem. The collaboration aims to help emerging ventures access mentorship, incubation support, and entrepreneurial expertise to accelerate technology development and commercialization.
IIT Kanpur and NSRCEL, the flagship business incubator of the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (IIM Bangalore), have partnered to accelerate the development of deep-tech startups and help emerging technologies move from research environments into commercially viable businesses. The institutions signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) bringing together technical research capabilities and entrepreneurial expertise to strengthen India’s startup ecosystem, particularly across defense, aerospace, and other strategic industries.
The collaboration addresses a critical challenge for deep-tech founders: translating complex technological breakthroughs into scalable products that meet real-world industry requirements. Unlike conventional startups, deep-tech ventures often depend on extended research and development cycles, specialized infrastructure, intellectual property development, and significant upfront capital. Moving from a laboratory prototype to a commercially deployable product also requires customer validation, regulatory compliance, manufacturing capabilities, and access to investors willing to support longer development timelines.
By combining IIT Kanpur’s research and engineering expertise with NSRCEL’s experience in entrepreneurship and business development, the partnership aims to create stronger pathways for technology-led ventures to navigate these challenges. The institutions will explore joint incubation and acceleration programs, co-incubation opportunities, knowledge exchange, and the sharing of entrepreneurial best practices. They will also strengthen engagement with industry participants, investors, and other stakeholders to help startups build commercial relationships and identify opportunities for market adoption.

A key focus of the partnership is the development of technologies relevant to defense and aerospace, sectors where domestic innovation can support strategic autonomy and reduce dependence on imported technologies. Access to research institutions, experienced mentors, industrial partners, and potential investors can help founders address these requirements while developing products that meet the needs of government agencies and commercial customers.

Dual-use innovations have applications in both civilian and military environments, creating opportunities for startups to expand their addressable markets while developing capabilities with strategic relevance. IIT Kanpur’s Startup Incubation and Innovation Centre has developed a technology-focused incubation network that connects research with commercialization, while NSRCEL supports entrepreneurs through incubation programs, mentorship, and business-building resources. Their combined expertise can help startups strengthen product development, refine business models, establish industry connections, and prepare for investment and expansion.
For India’s deep-tech ecosystem, the collaboration signals a stronger emphasis on converting research capabilities into market-ready businesses. Its long-term impact will depend on how effectively participating startups secure funding, validate their technologies, establish industry partnerships, and achieve commercial deployment. By connecting academic innovation with business execution, IIT Kanpur and NSRCEL aim to help promising technology ventures move closer to market adoption and contribute to India’s broader ambitions in strategic technology development.

articles.summary: What Trump’s new work permit, visa extension rules mean for Indians | HT Explainers  Hindustan TimesUS Department of Homeland Security removes 540-day grace period for immigrants after their work authorisation expires; here's what the new rules say  The Times of IndiaUS moves to end H-1B extension deference, automatic work permit renewals  OrissaPOSTUS proposes ending deference policy for H-1B extensions; Indian workers may face closer scrutiny  The Econom...
articles.full_text:
Washington is looking to scrap its policy of “deference” to prior visa approvals when reviewing extension applications, when no major details have changed.
The Donald Trump administration has rolled out two new immigration measures in recent days that could hit the ability of thousands of foreign professionals to work in the US.
The two developments emerged almost simultaneously. The government has finalised a rule that could cause some immigrants, including spouses of H-1B visa holders, to temporarily lose the right to work. Many foreign nationals need a work permit, known as an Employment Authorization Document (EAD), to work in the US.
Under the earlier policy, people who applied to renew their work permit before it expired could keep working for up to 540 days while US immigration authorities processed the application. The Trump administration has now said that foreign nationals whose work permits expire while their renewal is still being processed can no longer keep working until the new permit arrives. The rule, which took effect on a temporary basis last October, has now been made permanent.
Besides, the Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a new rule that could significantly increase scrutiny of previously routine visa extensions – including H-1B visas – and lead to longer wait times.
Washington is looking to scrap its policy of “deference” to prior visa approvals when reviewing extension applications, when no major details have changed.
Take, for instance, an Indian professional applying for a three-year extension of their H-1B visa while staying with the same employer. At present, immigration officials generally defer to the earlier approval instead of reviewing the case afresh, since the applicant already holds a visa and little has changed since the last application. The Trump administration now proposes to end this “deference,” which could add considerable uncertainty, paperwork and delays for foreign professionals.
Who will the regulations affect?
The first rule, on EADs, is likely to hit Indian spouses of H-1B visa holders hardest, since they (holders) need this work permit to take up a job in the US. As several feedback to US immigration authorities pointed out, the rule could cause significant loss of income to households even if they have followed immigration regulations faithfully and through no fault of their own due to simple processing delays.
The regulation could also hurt the US economy, costing employers an estimated $450 million in lost productivity and employee turnover over 18 months, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) estimate. It could also lead to a loss of $14.5 million in payroll taxes.
The second regulation could also impact a large number of Indian professionals in the US, with about two lakh extension petitions a year falling under the deference policy. According to immigration services firm Fragomen, such individuals could face higher rejection rates from immigration officials. US employers are likely to receive more requests for evidence when helping their foreign employees apply for visas.
Why is the Trump administration pursuing these policies?
For the first regulation, the Trump administration has argued that the earlier policy could lead to increased security threats.
“The automatic extension, therefore, poses a security vulnerability that could allow bad actors to continue to work and generate income to potentially finance nefarious activities that pose an imminent threat to the American public,” the DHS said in a notice released on Wednesday.
The department referred to a June 2025 case where a foreign national granted an automatic extension to their work permit attacked peaceful demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado to explain its move. Numerous individuals who participated in the public comments process pointed out that using a single case to change a policy was unfair given the disruption it would cause to many households.
The administration also justified ending the “deference” policy for foreign workers by arguing that it widens scope for more fraud and gaming of the immigration system. The present system allows workers who received visas fraudulently previously to easily receive visa extensions, it said.

New Delhi [India], October 15 (ANI): Private capital expenditure in India is likely to remain subdued in FY27 despite strong economic growth, leaving government spending and sectors such as energy transition and automation to drive investment, as per a report by Systematix Institutional Equities.
The report highlighted that private investment has failed to sustain its post-pandemic recovery despite several government measures aimed at encouraging companies to expand production capacity and increase spending.
However, "After peaking at Rs 2.6 billion per enterprise in FY23, private capex has fallen 38% to a provisional Rs 1.6 billion in FY26, with intended spending for FY27 showing no improvement," the report said.
According to a capital expenditure (capex) survey conducted by Systematix, "Overall, private capex per enterprise across 17 industries declined from Rs 1.8 billion in FY22 to Rs 1.6 billion in FY25 and remained unchanged in FY26."
The report noted that private investment witnessed a strong recovery after the pandemic, but provisional spending for FY26 and planned investment for FY27 stand at Rs 1.6 billion each, significantly below the levels recorded during the recovery period.
"The post-pandemic surge in private investment now appears less a durable capex upcycle and more a cyclical rebound from the extraordinary contraction of the pandemic years," it said.
The slowdown comes despite several government initiatives over the past decade to boost private investment, strengthen domestic manufacturing and revive capital expenditure.
Over the past decade, the government has introduced several measures to boost private investment, strengthen domestic manufacturing and revive capital expenditure, including higher government spending on infrastructure to encourage private investment, Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, easing foreign direct investment (FDI) rules and signing Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) to strengthen India's participation in global supply chains.
Additionally, the government introduced major corporate tax reforms in 2019, reducing effective tax rates to around 25.17 per cent for existing domestic companies and 17.01 per cent for new manufacturing firms. Companies opting for these lower tax rates were also exempted from the Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT).
These efforts were accompanied by monetary easing measures by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and improvements in corporate balance sheets.
The report further identified weak household demand and savings as major factors holding back private investment, as companies remain reluctant to expand production capacity without stronger consumer demand.
It stressed, "corporate investment ultimately relies on robust aggregate demand, squeezing household purchasing power while expecting private enterprises to build new capacities resulted in a persistent structural deadlock.
As a result, firms preferred utilizing cash flows for cost optimization, debt servicing, and automation rather than Greenfield capacity expansion."
Overall, "Unless demand conditions strengthen meaningfully and capacity utilization rises decisively, private capex is likely to remain a laggard, leaving public expenditure and a limited set of themes such as energy transition and automation to shoulder the burden of capital formation and growth," it said. (ANI)

Key Highlights
- The US FDA conducted an inspection of Neuland Laboratories' Unit 3 facility from 10 August 2026 to 14 August 2026, and has now issued the Establishment Inspection Report marking the matter closed.
- The company filed the update under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015, referencing its earlier letter dated 14 August 2026.
- The Unit 3 facility is located at Gaddapotharam Village, Jinnaram, Sangareddy District, and is a key active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing site for the company.
- The EIR closure indicates that the US FDA has concluded its review of the inspection findings without any further regulatory action being cited in the filing.
About the Company
Neuland Laboratories Limited (NSE:NEULANDLAB), headquartered in Hyderabad, Telangana, is an active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturer serving regulated markets including the United States, Europe, and Japan. The company operates multiple manufacturing units in Telangana and supplies APIs and custom synthesis services to global innovator and generic pharmaceutical firms across more than 80 countries.
Announcement in Detail
In its Regulation 30 filing dated 14 October 2026, Neuland Laboratories informed stock exchanges that the US FDA has issued an Establishment Inspection Report against the inspection conducted at its Unit 3 manufacturing facility at Gaddapotharam Village, Jinnaram, Sangareddy District, from 10 August 2026 to 14 August 2026. The company stated that the US FDA has concluded the inspection is "closed." The filing explicitly cross-referenced the company's earlier intimation to the exchanges dated 14 August 2026, which had disclosed the commencement and conduct of that inspection.
An Establishment Inspection Report is issued by the US FDA after reviewing the findings from a facility inspection and completing its internal assessment. The classification of an inspection as "closed" through an EIR signifies that the agency has completed its review of the site without escalating the matter to a Warning Letter or an Official Action Indicated status, based on the terms disclosed in this filing. No specific observations, citations, or corrective action commitments were detailed in the filing submitted to the exchanges.
Impact on Investors
Investors will note that the receipt of a closed EIR for Unit 3 resolves the regulatory uncertainty that arose when the inspection was first disclosed on 14 August 2026. The filing shows that the US FDA has concluded its review without citing further action in this communication, which removes a pending compliance overhang for this particular facility. Shareholders will observe that Unit 3 is among the company's manufacturing sites serving regulated export markets, making its regulatory standing directly relevant to the company's ability to supply US-market customers without interruption.
Sector / Market Context
India's pharmaceutical sector is among the most US FDA-inspected globally, with the agency routinely auditing Indian API and formulation facilities that supply the United States market. According to SEBI filings across the sector, EIR outcomes are closely tracked by institutional investors as indicators of a facility's compliance standing. The Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers has noted that Indian API manufacturers supply a significant share of generic drugs consumed in the United States, making US FDA inspection outcomes a material disclosure event for listed Indian pharma companies.

Speaking to Reuters at the Canadian High Commission in New Delhi, Anand said the proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with India was an important part of Ottawa's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships.
“Canada has a goal of doubling non-US trade over the next 10 years,” she said.
The push comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government looks to strengthen economic ties with the European Union, China and other markets, while continuing to work with Washington on trade, defence and security.
Anand said Canada and the European Union were expected to discuss closer cooperation in critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence at a summit later this month. The talks would build on their existing trade relationship under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
India trade deal gathers pace
Anand said negotiations were moving in the right direction on the proposed trade pact with India.
Indian trade negotiators visited Canada last week, whereas Canadian Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in India along with a business delegation.
The agreement has also come up in discussions between Carney and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Anand said. Modi is expected to travel to Canada in December.
Ottawa believes a trade agreement could help push annual bilateral trade in goods and services to $70 billion by 2030, more than double the $30.4 billion recorded in 2025.
Goods trade between the two countries stood at $10.9 billion in 2025. Canadian exports to India declined 26.5% from the previous year, but imports from India increased 18.9%.
Anand pointed to some recent deals as signs of growing economic cooperation between the two countries.
Among them is a C$2.6 billion uranium supply agreement signed earlier this year between Canadian company Cameco and India.
Another major development is Fairfax Financial Holdings' agreement to acquire a majority stake in IDBI Bank for ₹52,878 crore ($5.56 billion). The transaction is expected to become India's largest cross-border banking deal.
India, Canada seek to put diplomatic tensions behind them
The renewed focus on trade comes as India and Canada work to repair ties which has been disrupted by a diplomatic dispute over the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada.
The row had led to a sharp deterioration in relations between the two countries, complicating efforts to deepen their economic partnership.
Anand acknowledged that rebuilding relations would take time. She said national security and respect for the rule of law would remain important as both sides worked towards improving ties.
“We are speaking about our sovereignty and our resilience, and we need to continue to focus on that,” she said.

S. Jaishankar says India-US trade talks are progressing, highlights the strategic partnership with Washington and discusses China border stability and India-Russia ties.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has said that India-US trade negotiations are progressing in the right direction, with a potential trade deal currently being worked out by both sides. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, he said trade ministers from the two countries were engaged in negotiations and that the process had advanced considerably.
Jaishankar also addressed India's evolving relationship with the United States, the situation along the India-China border, trade imbalances with Beijing and India's engagement with Russia.
India-US Trade Deal Negotiations Advance
Jaishankar said negotiations between India and the United States had made significant progress and that a deal was being worked on.
He noted that trade ministers from both countries were involved in the process, adding that the negotiations had reached an advanced stage.
The remarks indicate continued efforts by New Delhi and Washington to reach a mutually acceptable trade arrangement. However, no final agreement was announced in the remarks provided.
India Must Recalibrate Ties with the United States
Responding to a question about Washington's changing approach to international relations, Jaishankar said the United States had repositioned itself and that every country needed to recalibrate and reset its relationship with it.
He also emphasised that India and the US share a strong strategic partnership.
His comments highlighted the need for countries to adapt their diplomatic and economic engagement as US policies and global relationships evolve.
India-China Relations Linked to Border Peace
On China, Jaishankar said disturbances to peace and tranquillity along the border would have consequences for bilateral relations.
He added that ties were moving towards normalcy as conditions in border areas stabilised. According to the minister, India and China had been able to restore peace and tranquillity along the border.
His remarks underscored the importance of maintaining stability in border regions for the broader relationship between the two countries.
Jaishankar Flags Unequal India-China Trade
The External Affairs Minister also raised concerns about India's trade relationship with China, describing the trade balance as heavily tilted in Beijing's favour.
He said India was not receiving a level playing field in the Chinese market.
The comments highlighted continuing concerns over trade imbalance and market access between the two Asian economies.
India-Russia Cooperation Amid the Ukraine War
Addressing questions about Russia, Jaishankar said India had not encountered any suggestion that the goods it procures from Russia came with Chinese technology.
He observed that the war in Ukraine had pushed Russia to turn more towards Asia. He added that it was in India's and the wider world's interest for Russia to have multiple options for engagement, describing India as a natural option in that context.
His remarks reflected India's approach of maintaining strategic and economic engagement with Russia while navigating a changing international environment.

articles.title: India should not turn Trump’s trade battle into a political cause | Policy Circle - Policy Circle
articles.summary: India should not turn Trump’s trade battle into a political cause | Policy Circle  Policy Circle
articles.full_text:
As far as US President Donald Trump is concerned, all his attempts at tariff diplomacy have been stymied by the local courts. Consequently, he has periodically used Section 301 (unfair trade practices) of the Trade Act of 1974 and Section 232 (national security) of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 to levy tariffs selectively.
Forced by court actions, Trump has taken recourse to Section 338, a 1930s instrument allowing blanket tariff protection against countries whose actions threaten US trade. But now he needs no such subterfuge. Congress has voted to give him full authority with the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, permitting Trump to impose 100 percent tariff action against countries importing Russian oil.
The general feeling in the media, therefore, seems to be that he will raise tariffs on India to 100 percent. However, this is not inevitable. Even if it happens, there will be some time lag, as in the case of pharmaceuticals, before implementation, giving India time to take corrective action.
More importantly, it has been argued that with the end of the Cold War in the 1990s, the US faced a new “cold war” challenge: China. However, the challenge was economic, not political. Despite the show of bravado, US tariff action on the basis of the new Act is already on hold, while talks with President Xi Jin Ping were on.
READ I India-US trade deal comes under the shadow of Ukraine war
Trump, India, and lessons from China
What is known is that China has reduced its trade dependence on the US market over the last decade or so, and any US action would hurt American consumers more than the Chinese. Trump knows this, given looming US inflation and legislative elections in November, where inflation is the main focus.
Both Trump and Xi also know that given their vast reliance on each other, a trade war would be mutually destructive. With the conclusion of the US-China trade agreement, the terms are broadly on expected lines: US-China to cut tariffs on about $60 billion in trade, with tariff cuts on US goods like corn, wheat, frozen meat (but not soya), while US cuts some duties on small appliances, toys, holiday decorations, and children’s car seats.
More important was the decision to cooperate on the risks of AI for both countries, with some future dialogue on “super intelligence”. So, no fireworks and no “trade Armageddon”, as Trump himself boasted at one point.
In the final analysis, Trump is a businessman first and politician later. Xi has already diverted China’s exports to the US to other countries, and Trump has achieved a reduction in his trade deficit with China from about $297 billion in 2024 to $200 billion in 2025. So why a mutually destructive war?
How should India respond, given that it is a major importer of Russian oil? Should India make some concessions in the ongoing trade discussions?
There has been speculation that the recent changes in the UPI system were intended to mollify the US. Even if so, this is unlikely to work, as it does not address the larger issue of Russian sanctions, which is what the Congress legislation is all about. The UPI issue is probably more closely related to the hidden consumer subsidy in place since UPI’s early days, which has now outlived its utility in incentivising people to adopt digital payment channels. That is a separate issue requiring a full article.
The Indo-US trade agreement
Here again, the government seems to have jumped the gun, if media reports are to be believed, by arguing that a 100 percent duty would harm bilateral political relations.
The US action against Canada, Brazil and Mexico have shown that Trump could not care less.
China is an economic worry: a failed agreement would have thrown domestic US inflation into greater disarray, apart from being a setback for the IT ecosystem. Hence, no action was likely against China, the most important buyer of Russian oil. International politics is not on Trump’s radar.
Yet Indian spokesmen continue to highlight what the use of this tariff implies for political relations. But for Trump, the issue is economic, not political. Why are we determined to make it political?
On the other hand, it pays India to stay low-key on this issue because of its services trade with the US. India’s total goods trade with the US is about $140 billion, with a $33.9 billion surplus. Yet India’s trade with its other major partners—the EU, UAE and China—is about $390 billion. India must, therefore, slowly shift its trade policy in those directions.
There is some evidence that this is already happening. As far as commodity trade is concerned, the US is not the only kid on the block.
The recent focus on FTAs — with the UK, Australia, Oman and European Free Trade Association (EFTA), and the deal concluded with the EU — is one way trade policy must change, and seems to be changing.
While FTAs per se do not create trade—there is plenty of empirical evidence on this—they allow member countries to move towards higher levels of cooperation, including foreign investment and regulatory systems.
The focus on FTAs is, therefore, an indication of a clear change in global economic and political engagement. This is clearly visible in the recent FTAs that India has been negotiating. India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which was signed on 10 March 2024 in New Delhi and came into force on 1 October 2025, exemplifies this. The agreement includes investment commitments by the EFTA members of $100 billion over 15 years, tied to tariff concessions.
The recent FTAs have also focused on easing the market access for India’s services sector. This includes more favourable regulations for mobility of Indian service providers in sectors including, information technology and related services, financial services, healthcare, education, and consultancy services among others. Similarly, services related commitments are also part of India-EFTA TEPA as well as the India-EU FTA concluded in January, this year.
More broadly, trade in services has been growing at about 6.22 percent in 2025-26 and 13.36 percent in 2024-25. The US is the dominant source of revenues here, and a $200 billion surplus is what keeps the overall current account deficit (CAD) to a manageable 0.6 percent of GDP.
Why would India want to endanger this? It is clear that global focus today is on economics, not politics. This delicately balanced apple cart should not be overturned.
Manoj Pant is Visiting Professor at the Shiv Nadar Institution of Eminence, Delhi-NCR, and a former Vice-Chancellor of the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade. M Rahul is an Assistant Professor at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi and was formerly with the Indian Economic Service and the Reserve Bank of India.
