articles.title: UPSC Editorial Analysis: India’s Growth vs. Jobs Debate - INSIGHTS IAS
articles.summary: UPSC Editorial Analysis: India’s Growth vs. Jobs Debate  INSIGHTS IAS
articles.full_text:
General Studies-3; Topic: Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilization of resources, growth, development and employment.
Introduction
- India’s GDP is expanding at around 6.5% to 7.5% per year, making it the fastest-growing major economy in the world.
- The Problem: This economic growth is not producing enough stable, well-paying jobs. Economists describe this as job-deficient growth or jobless growth.
What the Official Numbers Really Mean
Official statistics often appear contradictory.
- Low Headline Unemployment:
  - The government’s Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) reports a low overall unemployment rate of around 3.1% to 3.2%.
  - Why it is misleading: The survey uses the “Usual Status” measure. If a person worked for even 30 days in the entire year—even unpaid on a family farm—they are officially counted as employed.
- High Youth Joblessness:
  - According to the International Labour Organization (ILO) India Employment Report, young people make up nearly 83% of India’s total unemployed population.
  - College graduates between 15 and 29 face unemployment rates between 25% and 30%.
- The Informality Trap:
  - Nearly 90% of all jobs in India are informal. Workers have no written contracts, no pension, and no paid medical leave.
  - Only about 1 in 5 Indian workers earns a regular monthly salary.
- Disguised Unemployment in Agriculture:
  - Around 45% of Indians still work in farming, but agriculture contributes only about 16% of the country’s GDP.
  - Many people working on family farms add almost no extra economic output. They work there simply because cities lack factory jobs for them.
Why Is This Happening? (Core Reasons)
- India Skipped the “Factory Stage”
  - The Normal Path (e.g., China, South Korea): Farms -> Labour-intensive factories (garments, shoes, toys) -> High-tech services.
  - India’s Path: Farms -> Directly to Services (IT, software, finance).
  - The Result: High-tech services make a lot of money, but they require advanced degrees and cannot hire millions of semi-skilled workers.
- Machines Replacing People
  - Even when modern manufacturing grows in India, companies invest heavily in machines, robots, and automated assembly rather than hiring large workforces. This is called capital-intensive growth.
- The “Missing Middle” Among Small Businesses
  - India has a few giant corporations and millions of tiny corner shops, but very few medium-sized factories employing 100 to 500 workers.
  - Complex labour regulations and tax paperwork discourage small businesses from growing larger.
- The Skills Gap
  - The India Skills Report regularly points out that nearly half of college graduates are not directly employable because college syllabi focus on memorisation rather than real industry skills.
- Women Are Left Out
  - Only about 1 in 4 urban women works in the formal labour force.
  - Safety concerns, lack of reliable public transport, and the heavy burden of domestic and childcare duties keep women out of paid jobs.
Government Policies
| Initiative | What It Tries to Do | Where It Falls Short | 
| PLI Scheme (Production-Linked Incentive) | Pays cash subsidies to companies that manufacture goods in India. | Mostly helps high-tech, machine-heavy sectors (smartphones, pharma), not job-heavy sectors like textiles. | 
| MUDRA Yojana | Gives collateral-free small business loans. | Most loans are tiny (under ₹50,000). They help people open tea stalls or small retail shops for survival, but rarely create jobs for others. | 
| Skill India / PMKVY | Provides short vocational training courses. | Training often does not match what local factories actually need; placement rates remain modest. | 
| Gig Economy Growth | Delivery apps and ride-sharing provide quick earning options. | These are insecure gig jobs without health insurance, minimum wage guarantees, or retirement benefits. | 
Way Forward
- Support Heavy Job Creators: 
  - Give tax benefits and subsidies to sectors that naturally require large numbers of hands: garments, leather, footwear, food processing, and tourism.
- Fix the MSME Ecosystem:
  - Ensure small suppliers get paid on time by large buyers using digital platforms like TReDS.
Simplify factory regulations so small firms are not penalised for growing larger.
- Launch an Urban Jobs Guarantee:
  - Create an urban version of MGNREGA focused on city maintenance, green spaces, and urban water bodies to support young people during economic downturns.
- Dual Education (Classroom + Factory):
  - Adopt the apprenticeship model: students should spend half their time in vocational institutes and the other half learning on factory floors.
- Support Working Women:
  - Build state-subsidised creches (daycares) near industrial parks and ensure safe, affordable public transport between suburbs and work districts.
- Provide Social Security for Gig Workers:
  - Set up a welfare fund for delivery drivers and app-based workers, funded by a small fee on app transactions.
Conclusion
- To harness its closing demographic window, India must convert high GDP growth into inclusive development by expanding labour-intensive manufacturing, empowering MSMEs, and ensuring social protection for all workers.

articles.title: Festive demand may hold up, but consumer volume growth likely to moderate: Aditi Nayar, ICRA - bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: Festive demand may hold up, but consumer volume growth likely to moderate: Aditi Nayar, ICRA  bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
India's consumer spending is likely to see more moderate growth in the second half of the current fiscal year despite resilient demand so far, as the impact of earlier tax cuts fades from comparisons and rising food and fuel costs threaten household budgets, ICRA Chief Economist Aditi Nayar said.
New Delhi [India], October 14 (ANI): India's consumer spending is likely to see more moderate growth in the second half of the current fiscal year despite resilient demand so far, as the impact of earlier tax cuts fades from comparisons and rising food and fuel costs threaten household budgets, ICRA Chief Economist Aditi Nayar said.
Speaking to ANI, Nayar said income tax rationalisation and GST rationalisation had supported consumption over the past year and a half. However, the strong growth following GST changes is likely to make comparisons tougher in the coming months.
Nayar said consumer growth had remained resilient, with high-frequency indicators staying strong despite the West Asia crisis. However, consumer sentiment indices published by the Reserve Bank of India for both rural and urban areas had been pointing downwards throughout the calendar year.
Food inflation and crude oil prices will be key factors determining the outlook for household spending. Nayar said a further rise in food prices following a weak monsoon could affect household budgets, disposable income, inflation expectations and consumer sentiment.
"Things like food, the percolation of food price pressures to the inflationary expectations and consumer demand is very, very quick," she said.
She added that persistently high commodity prices could force more producers to pass on higher costs to consumers, putting further pressure on demand.
The other major risk is a sustained increase in crude oil prices that leads to meaningful hikes in retail petrol and diesel prices.
"If that is the case, then definitely I think consumer sentiment will take a greater hit. Otherwise, we are hoping that the resilience that we have seen so far can continue," Nayar said.
On the broader economic outlook, ICRA expects India's GDP to grow by 7.1 per cent in the current fiscal year. In an adverse scenario where crude oil prices do not correct, growth could be around 6.8 per cent, she said.
Nayar also expects at least one more rate hike by the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee in December, adding that bond yields are likely to remain elevated amid inflation risks, higher global yields and elevated crude oil prices.
Higher bond yields could shift corporate borrowing towards banks, which currently have surplus liquidity, rather than the bond market over the next couple of quarters. She said elevated yields were unlikely to derail capacity expansion plans already underway, although a broader recovery in private investment may take longer.
Private investment remains concentrated in renewable energy, data centres, electric vehicles, cement, steel, hotels, aviation and hospitals, while investment remains limited in export-oriented sectors and those facing strong competition from Chinese imports.
Nayar further said recent RBI measures to support the rupee were in the right direction. A sustained decline in crude oil prices to USD 90-95 per barrel could also ease pressure on the currency, although uncertainty and foreign institutional investor flows remain factors to watch. (ANI)

articles.title: Tata's Chip Bet: A Long-Term Play for India's Growth, Says Chandrasekaran - Rediff
articles.summary: Tata's Chip Bet: A Long-Term Play for India's Growth, Says Chandrasekaran  Rediff
articles.full_text:
Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran asserts that the group's significant investment in semiconductors is a strategic, long-term commitment vital for India's future growth and domestic consumption, rather than a short-term financial gamble.
Key Points
- Tata's semiconductor investment is a long-term strategic move, not focused on short-term returns, driven by the belief that chips are fundamentally required for India's domestic consumers and overall growth.
- Chandrasekaran emphasised India's potential to become a significant player in global supply chains, leveraging its talent and domestic market, though partnerships are needed for technology acquisition.
- Businesses must build resilience into their operations rather than solely optimising for efficiency in the current unpredictable global environment, which includes geopolitical tensions, AI disruption, and supply-chain issues.
- Tata Electronics is establishing a fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat, in partnership with ASML Holding NV, and a semiconductor facility in Assam, expected to produce 48 million chips daily.
- Chandrasekaran highlighted the unprecedented simultaneous disruptions globally, including geopolitical tensions, AI, and supply-chain issues, making the current environment unique.
For Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran, the group's bet on semiconductors is not about getting the numbers right over the next two or three years, but about investing in a sector that will be critical to India's long-term growth.
He said the group's experience had shown that investments made with the country's needs in mind had consistently proved to be the right decisions.
"Whether we get semiconductor chips right or we get the numbers right in two-three years, that is not the point.
"Chips are going to be fundamentally required for domestic consumers," Chandrasekaran said.
He was speaking at a panel discussion titled The End of Predictability at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026.
He said this investment philosophy had encouraged the Tata group to venture into the semiconductor and electronics sectors.
India's Global Manufacturing Opportunity
Underlining India's opportunity in global manufacturing, he said the country had the talent and domestic market to become an important player in global supply chains.
"We have the talent, domestic market, we can play a part in every global supply chain.
"We need partnerships because we do not have all the technologies."
He also cautioned that while companies must be willing to take risks, they should keep an eye on their balance sheets.
"You have to be careful, and keep an eye on the balance sheet.
"One cannot be reckless. We need to see where the demand is," he said.
Tata Electronics is establishing a fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat, in partnership with Dutch company ASML Holding NV.
The company is also setting up a semiconductor facility in Assam, which is expected to produce 48 million chips a day.
Navigating Global Uncertainty
Asked how the current global uncertainty differed from past events, Chandrasekaran said this was the first time so many disruptions were occurring simultaneously.
These included geopolitical tensions, disruption from artificial intelligence, and commodity and supply-chain disruptions.
"At the same time the connected world is trying to decouple itself.
"And tackling all of these things now is unique," he added.
He identified technology as a major near-term disruptor, particularly when it fell into the hands of bad actors, and pointed to the labour restructuring that would eventually follow.
"The other thing that I worry about is the war situation.
"We are opening a war in every situation, and nothing is getting closed," he added.
Building Business Resilience
Chandrasekaran said businesses should build resilience into their operations rather than focus solely on efficiency in an unpredictable environment.
He argued that the two were not mutually exclusive.
"In a highly unpredictable, volatile environment, optimising for efficiency is definitely not the right thing," he said.
"I believe that if you design for resilience in an unpredictable environment, actually you are optimising for efficiency."
He cited shortages of magnets that could disrupt vehicle production and the cyberattack that affected Jaguar Land Rover, saying the company had lost almost six weeks of production due to the incident.
The group had also faced an air crash and supply-chain disruptions, he said, but still expected to deliver double-digit growth while maintaining margins.
He did not specify the period or provide financial projections to quantify the outlook.
Chandrasekaran said he had asked companies across the group to define resilience for their own businesses rather than adopt a single framework.

articles.title: India, U.S. ironing out differences on trade deal; nearing 'landing point': Jaishankar - The Hindu
articles.summary: India, U.S. ironing out differences on trade deal; nearing 'landing point': Jaishankar  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
India and the U.S. are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a "landing point," External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has said, while noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.
The External Affairs Minister's comments on the trade negotiations came over a week after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks on the trade deal have reached a "plateau".
"I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public," he said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Tuesday evening when asked about the status of the negotiations between the two sides.
Mr. Jaishankar said India's trade minister, the US Trade Representative (USTR) and other officials concerned are engaged in talks to move forward on the bilateral trade pact.
"When countries negotiate with an economy like the United States, obviously one part of it is what you work out between yourselves and the U.S., and one part of it is how do you fare vis-a-vis competitive economies.
"And that part of it is not entirely clear because not everybody has worked out a deal. I think people, the trade ministers, USTR (U.S. Trade Representative), and our Commerce and Industry Minister are there working on that. They're ironing it out," he said.
"My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point," Mr. Jaishankar said.
India and the U.S. have been in talks since early 2025 on the proposed trade pact to address tariff friction, eliminate non-tariff barriers, and boost bilateral market access.
India is seeking better tariffs than its competitors for its goods in the U.S. market.
Earlier this month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the United States and India were working to finalise a bilateral trade deal, but an agreement was not imminent.
Mr. Greer said the two sides identified the issues that remained unresolved and were working towards an agreement.
In his remarks, Mr. Jaishankar also delved into Washington's new approach on economic engagement.
"The U.S. has a fundamentally different approach to the use of tariffs. But even that is a symptom of something else. The US is today determined to re-industrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy," he said.
"That's what the whole tariff debate is about. And the two are connected: access to the American economy and the re-industrialisation of America. Therefore, what is happening is every significant economy is getting into a negotiation with the United States on this issue," he said.
"We're not alone in this. In our case, we are pretty far advanced in that process of negotiation," he said.
Mr. Jaishankar also noted that the U.S. is revising the terms of its alliances and treaty relationships and that the sentiment is most strongly being felt in Europe, and to some extent, in some countries in East Asia.
"We have many issues we are working on with the United States, but we don't have an issue of the terms of alliance because we are not officially an ally. We are a country which has a strong strategic partnership with the US, but a strategic partnership is a partnership; it's not an alliance," he added.
"In our case, for the last 20-odd years, we have worked out what we felt were convergences, overlaps, shared common interests with the US, and we had agreed that we would pursue that. I don't think that has fundamentally changed," he said.
The India-U.S. relations witnessed a major downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year and President Donald Trump made assertions regarding his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military clashes of May 2025 that drew sharp reaction from Indian officials.
Washington's new immigration policy and its decision to increase H1B visa fee also contributed to the slide in India-U.S. ties.
The ties came under fresh strain after the US decided to restrict a key green-card processing programme for major global and Indian IT firms, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.

articles.title: India-US ties ‘very substantive, consequential’, says Piyush Goyal amid trade deal uncertainty - Livemint
articles.summary: India-US ties ‘very substantive, consequential’, says Piyush Goyal amid trade deal uncertainty  Livemint
articles.full_text:
Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Wednesday that India’s ties with the US are ‘very good,’ even as trade tensions simmer ever since President Donald Trump claimed he helped mediate an end to armed clashes with Pakistan last year.
“I don’t see any problem as we speak,” Goyal said Wednesday at the New Economy Forum in New Delhi, responding to a question on whether India’s relationship with the US would improve under a different administration.
The forum is being organized by Bloomberg Media Group, a division of Bloomberg LP, the parent company of Bloomberg News.
“The relationship with the US that India enjoys is very substantive, is very consequential for the world, being two large democracies,” the minister was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
The remarks come as India and the US have struggled to hammer out a trade deal during prolonged negotiations and after relations were soured by Trump’s punitive tariffs. Ties were further dented by the president’s comments on India’s brief armed conflict with Pakistan last year that breached diplomatic norms.
The latest flashpoint with Washington comes after the suspension of some of India’s biggest IT services businesses as well as Microsoft Corp. and Adobe Inc. from a longstanding immigration initiative as part of a crackdown on alleged abuse of the H-1B worker visa system.
Vice President JD Vance urged US firms to hire more US workers and to “stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do.”
India’s government branded the comments “deeply offensive.” An indentured servant is associated in India with a colonial-era system in which workers were forced into labor on plantations and farms overseas under exploitative conditions.
India and the US have been in talks since early 2025 on the proposed trade pact to address tariff friction, eliminate non-tariff barriers, and boost bilateral market access.
India is seeking better tariffs than its competitors for its goods in the US market.

“The US and India have a very, very consequential relationship, and it’s only going to get better, irrespective of changes in political thinking, whether in India or in the US,” he said. “The United States and India continue to have a very close relationship, and we continue to engage with them on so many tracks,” including in defense, working toward ensuring open supply chains on technology, on goods, on services.

“We are open to all countries around the world as long as we get a fair deal, as long as we are ensured continuity in the engagement, and as long as the geopolitical situation does not deteriorate,” Goyal said.
On Tuesday, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said that India and the United States are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a ‘landing point.’ The minister noted that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.
The external affairs minister's comments on the trade negotiations came over a week after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks on the trade deal have reached a "plateau".
"I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public," Jaishankar said on Tuesday evening when asked about the status of the negotiations between the two sides.

New Delhi [India], October 14 (ANI): India's consumer spending is likely to see more moderate growth in the second half of the current fiscal year despite resilient demand so far, as the impact of earlier tax cuts fades from comparisons and rising food and fuel costs threaten household budgets, ICRA Chief Economist Aditi Nayar said.
Speaking to ANI, Nayar said income tax rationalisation and GST rationalisation had supported consumption over the past year and a half. However, the strong growth following GST changes is likely to make comparisons tougher in the coming months.
"We do expect that there is going to be a moderation in volume growth across a lot of sectors," she said.
Nayar said consumer growth had remained resilient, with high-frequency indicators staying strong despite the West Asia crisis. However, consumer sentiment indices published by the Reserve Bank of India for both rural and urban areas had been pointing downwards throughout the calendar year.
"Despite that, so far the high frequencies have held up, but we do think that there is going to be a more moderated kind of volume growth going ahead," she said.
Food inflation and crude oil prices will be key factors determining the outlook for household spending. Nayar said a further rise in food prices following a weak monsoon could affect household budgets, disposable income, inflation expectations and consumer sentiment.
"Things like food, the percolation of food price pressures to the inflationary expectations and consumer demand is very, very quick," she said.
She added that persistently high commodity prices could force more producers to pass on higher costs to consumers, putting further pressure on demand.
The other major risk is a sustained increase in crude oil prices that leads to meaningful hikes in retail petrol and diesel prices.
"If that is the case, then definitely I think consumer sentiment will take a greater hit. Otherwise, we are hoping that the resilience that we have seen so far can continue," Nayar said.
On the broader economic outlook, ICRA expects India's GDP to grow by 7.1 per cent in the current fiscal year. In an adverse scenario where crude oil prices do not correct, growth could be around 6.8 per cent, she said.
Nayar also expects at least one more rate hike by the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee in December, adding that bond yields are likely to remain elevated amid inflation risks, higher global yields and elevated crude oil prices.
Higher bond yields could shift corporate borrowing towards banks, which currently have surplus liquidity, rather than the bond market over the next couple of quarters. She said elevated yields were unlikely to derail capacity expansion plans already underway, although a broader recovery in private investment may take longer.
Private investment remains concentrated in renewable energy, data centres, electric vehicles, cement, steel, hotels, aviation and hospitals, while investment remains limited in export-oriented sectors and those facing strong competition from Chinese imports.
Nayar further said recent RBI measures to support the rupee were in the right direction. A sustained decline in crude oil prices to USD 90-95 per barrel could also ease pressure on the currency, although uncertainty and foreign institutional investor flows remain factors to watch. (ANI)

articles.title: 'Heading Towards a Landing Point': EAM Jaishankar on India-US Trade Deal Negotiations - Republic World
articles.summary: 'Heading Towards a Landing Point': EAM Jaishankar on India-US Trade Deal Negotiations  Republic World
articles.full_text:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said India-US trade deal negotiations are approaching a possible conclusion, with officials working to resolve outstanding issues. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer also indicated talks were in the final stretch, though an immediate announcement is not expected.
New Delhi: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Tuesday said that negotiations on the India-US trade deal were progressing towards a possible conclusion, adding that both sides were working to resolve outstanding issues.
Speaking in a conversation with John Micklethwait, Editor-in-Chief at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in Delhi, Jaishankar said that discussions were ongoing between the trade officials of both countries, while noting that he would not disclose details of the negotiations publicly.
"I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public. It's a small select order... When countries negotiate with an economy like the United States, obviously one part of it is what you work out between yourselves and the US, and one part of it is how you fare vis-a-vis competitive economies. That part of it is not entirely clear because not everybody has worked out the deal. I think people, the trade ministers, USTR, and our Commerce and Industry Minister are there, working on that. They're ironing it out. My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point," Jaishankar said.
The External Affairs Minister also said that the United States had changed the manner and basis on which it engaged with the world, requiring countries to reassess their bilateral relationships.
"I never said it was easy. So I said, engage America, manage China... In 2020, I was looking at a world. I was looking at Brexit, Donald Trump's election, the backlash against globalisation, and kind of partly forecasting, partly analysing, where's the world going and how does India react to this? So your question, in a way: how difficult is it to engage America? You make it sound as though we are the only country having problems with the United States. The reality is the United States has repositioned itself. It's changed the manner in which it engages the world, the basis on which it engages the world. I think every country, in a way, has to recalculate and reset its relationship with the United States," he said.
Jaishankar further explained that India's relationship with the United States was based on a strategic partnership rather than a formal alliance, adding that the underlying areas of convergence between the two countries had not fundamentally changed.
"I think a lot of what America is revising are its alliances, the terms of its treaty relationships. So the sentiment is most strongly felt vis-a-vis Europe, to some extent, some countries in East Asia. We have many issues we are working on with the United States, but we don't have an issue of the terms of alliance because we are not officially an ally. We are a country which has a strong strategic partnership with the US, but a strategic partnership is a partnership; it's not an alliance. In our case, for the last 20-odd years, we have worked out what we felt were convergences, overlaps, shared common interests with the US, and we had agreed that we would pursue that. I don't think that has fundamentally changed," he said.
The External Affairs Minister also pointed to Washington's changing approach towards tariffs, linking it to the US objective of rebuilding its industrial base and resetting the terms of access to its economy.
"The US has a fundamentally different approach to the use of tariffs. But even that is a symptom of something else. The US is today determined to reindustrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy. That's what the whole tariff debate is about. And the two are connected: access to the American economy and the reindustrialisation of America. Therefore, what is happening is every significant economy is getting into a negotiation with the United States on this issue. We're not alone in this. In our case, we are pretty far advanced in that process of negotiation," Jaishankar added.
Earlier in October, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that negotiations on the bilateral trade agreement between India and the United States are nearing their final phase, though a final announcement is not imminent.
Responding to a question from ANI at the 2026 G20 Trade Ministers Meeting, Greer said talks were in the "short strokes", an American expression for the final stretch of a task. "I think we're toward the end of it," he said.
Greer said Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump had a "very constructive call" on Wednesday morning, US time, and may speak again soon to assess progress. "My sense is that the President and the Prime Minister may have another call very soon on this just to assess progress and where we are," he told ANI.
He cautioned against expecting a quick announcement, but said both sides had mapped out the core issues. "I don't think there's something imminent, but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points, and we're working diligently toward them," Greer said.
Describing his meeting with Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, Greer said, "We had a very constructive conversation, Minister Goyal and myself. Our staff is meeting right now, since they're in the country and we're here. We are continually trying to finish the trade deal with India."
Goyal met Greer on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee. Sharing details on X, Goyal said he "had a productive discussion with USTR Greer towards early conclusion of a mutually beneficial interim agreement under the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement".

articles.summary: DHL Plans Dholera Semiconductor Warehouse as Race for India’s Chip Logistics Heats Up  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Summary
DHL plans to set up its first dedicated semiconductor warehouse in India at Dholera, Gujarat, joining Japan’s NX Group in positioning for logistics contracts tied to the country’s emerging chip manufacturing base. The move reflects growing competition among global logistics operators to serve fabs, assembly plants and their suppliers as India builds its semiconductor supply chain.
Article
Dholera: Global logistics major DHL has entered India’s semiconductor logistics market with plans to set up its first dedicated semiconductor warehouse in Dholera, Gujarat, according to a Mint report. The move puts DHL alongside Japan’s NX Group in a growing contest to serve India’s chip manufacturing ecosystem.
As India’s first fabs and assembly units move towards production, international freight and supply chain operators are positioning themselves to win high-value logistics and infrastructure contracts.
Why is Dholera the focus?
Dholera is home to India’s first front-end semiconductor fab, being built by Tata Electronics with Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation (PSMC) inside the Dholera Special Investment Region. The project is backed by an investment of about ₹91,000 crore and targets chips from 110nm to 28nm.
Nearby, Sanand has become a cluster for assembly, testing and packaging. It hosts Micron’s ATMP plant, Kaynes Semicon’s OSAT unit and a CG Power-Renesas-Stars Microelectronics joint venture.
What is NX Group doing?
NX Group, formerly Nippon Express, has moved early. It signed an MoU with the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) at SEMICON India 2026, held in New Delhi from September 17 to 19, to work on logistics and supply chain solutions for the sector.
The Japanese group plans to open a dedicated semiconductor logistics centre in the Dholera area in 2027 and aims to raise its India sales to ¥60 billion by fiscal 2028. It currently runs 103 locations and 60 warehouses across 39 cities in India.
NX has also signed an MoU with Japan’s Nagase to build a supply chain for front-end semiconductor manufacturing materials in Dholera. The partnership focuses on dangerous goods management, just-in-time delivery and proximity-based supply networks.
What does semiconductor logistics involve?
Chip supply chains demand far more than conventional warehousing. Fabs depend on a steady flow of specialty chemicals, gases, wafers and precision equipment, much of it hazardous or highly sensitive to vibration, temperature, humidity and contamination. Finished chips and wafers are high-value, time-critical cargo that often move by air.
Providers must offer cleanroom-grade storage, temperature-controlled handling, secure bonded inventory, dangerous goods expertise and tightly integrated just-in-time delivery. Such capabilities are scarce in India today, creating an opening for global players with experience in established chip hubs in Asia, Europe and the US.
Why does it matter for Indian logistics?
DHL’s entry signals that global logistics majors see India’s semiconductor programme moving from announcements to operations. Competition between DHL, NX and others should speed up the creation of specialised facilities near Dholera and Sanand, raising the bar for handling standards across India’s logistics sector.
For ports and airports in Gujarat, rising semiconductor activity could bring demand for specialised import handling of chemicals and equipment, along with export flows of finished chips and modules. Early movers that lock in relationships with fabs and their suppliers are likely to gain a lasting advantage as India’s chip ecosystem scales up.

It requires cleanroom-grade storage, temperature and humidity control, dangerous goods handling and just-in-time delivery for sensitive, high-value cargo.

Rubio to visit India next week as Jaishankar says trade talks near landing point
The US Department of State announced that Marco Rubio will first travel to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to participate in the C5+1 Ministerial with the five Central Asian republics before heading to India. This will be Rubio's second visit to India since May, when he attended the Quad Foreign Ministers' meeting.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will visit India next week, travelling to Mumbai and Gujarat's Jamnagar as Washington looks to deepen energy cooperation, strategic ties and commercial engagement with New Delhi despite ongoing differences over trade and India's purchases of Russian oil.
The US Department of State announced Tuesday that Rubio will first travel to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to participate in the C5+1 Ministerial with the five Central Asian republics before heading to India. This will be Rubio's second visit to India since May, when he attended the Quad Foreign Ministers' meeting hosted by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi.
In India, Rubio will meet senior government officials to discuss the bilateral strategic partnership, regional and global developments, and expanded energy cooperation. He will also engage with business leaders to promote investment and economic ties, according to the State Department.
The announcement comes as Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said Tuesday that India-US trade negotiations were moving towards a resolution, even as Washington’s changing trade policies force countries to reassess their economic relationships with the United States.
“My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point,” Jaishankar said during a conversation with Bloomberg News Editor-in-Chief John Micklethwait at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
Jaishankar said the United States was seeking to rebuild domestic industries and reset the terms on which other countries access its market. He indicated that India was evaluating the proposed agreement in the context of the terms Washington was offering other trading partners.
“The United States has repositioned itself,” Jaishankar said, adding that countries needed to “recalculate and reset” their relationships with Washington as its approach to international engagement changed.
The remarks offer a cautiously optimistic assessment of the trade negotiations, which have faced renewed uncertainty over tariffs, market access and the competitive position of Indian exports.
FROM MAY'S OPTIMISM TO RENEWED TRADE UNCERTAINTY
Rubio’s forthcoming visit follows his four-day trip to India in May, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Jaishankar for discussions on trade, energy, defence, maritime security and regional developments.
During his May 24 meeting with Jaishankar, Rubio expressed confidence that the two countries could reach a durable trade agreement. He said the negotiations had made substantial progress and that Washington hoped to conclude an agreement beneficial to both sides.
Jaishankar, meanwhile, called for an early conclusion to the interim trade agreement, describing it as an important step towards a comprehensive bilateral trade deal first envisaged during Modi’s February 2025 visit to Washington.
The May discussions also covered energy diversification, nuclear cooperation, critical minerals, technology and visa-related challenges faced by Indian travellers. Rubio subsequently met Modi, discussing trade and energy, and conveyed an invitation from President Donald Trump for the Indian prime minister to visit the White House.
Rubio’s May visit also included engagement with the Quad, the strategic grouping comprising the United States, India, Japan and Australia, underscoring the wider geopolitical significance of the relationship.
TRADE DEAL REMAINS A KEY TEST
Despite the optimism expressed in May, negotiations have continued amid changes in US tariff policy and disagreements over market access. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on October 5 that the talks had reached a plateau, with further concessions becoming increasingly difficult for both sides.
The United States has sought to address its trade imbalance and expand access to the Indian market, while New Delhi has sought terms that protect sensitive domestic sectors and keep Indian exporters competitive against rival economies.
Jaishankar’s latest comments suggest that discussions are continuing and that a resolution remains possible. However, his remarks do not amount to an announcement that a final agreement has been concluded.
Rubio’s October visit will therefore provide another opportunity for Washington and New Delhi to advance their economic and strategic partnership, with energy cooperation explicitly identified by the State Department as an important part of the agenda.

IBM and the MeitY Startup Hub have signed an MoU to bolster India's deep-tech startup ecosystem. The partnership will provide startups with access to IBM's enterprise technology, mentorship, and industry connections to help them scale globally.
IBM and MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), an initiative of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to help India's deep-tech startups develop, test and commercialise their technologies through access to enterprise technology, mentorship and industry connections.
The collaboration aims to help startups working in areas such as enterprise artificial intelligence, hybrid cloud and quantum computing validate their solutions and scale them for Indian and global markets.
Details of the Collaboration
Under the agreement, startups will get access to IBM's enterprise technology portfolio, technical guidance, skilling programmes and opportunities to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors.
The two organisations will also explore enterprise proof-of-concept projects to help startups test their technologies against real business requirements.
Fostering Indigenous Capabilities
Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO of MeitY Startup Hub, said the partnership would strengthen domestic technology capabilities and encourage entrepreneurship. "Through this collaboration with IBM, we aim to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities, foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat," he said.
Technology Access and Strategic Initiatives
The partnership will cover technologies and platforms including IBM watsonx, an enterprise AI and data platform, IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises, and IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty. Startups will also receive technical orientation on hybrid cloud, quantum computing, security and automation solutions.
The organisations will jointly explore initiatives across sectors such as banking, finance, government and industry, with a focus on founder mentorship, open-source ecosystem development and technical training. A key priority will be identifying and supporting promising innovators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities to broaden access to India's deep-tech startup ecosystem.
From Innovation to Real-World Impact
Sandip Patel, Managing Director of IBM India and South Asia, said the partnership aimed to help startups move from innovation towards practical applications. "Together with MeitY Startup Hub, we aim to help founders innovate faster, scale responsibly, and build solutions that address both national and global challenges – turning promising innovation into real-world impact," he said.
The MoU complements IBM Ventures' existing engagements in India, which support enterprise technology startups through capital, access to IBM's global network and connections with industry experts. The collaboration is intended to expand opportunities for startups to connect with potential customers, investors and industry partners, helping them develop and scale technology solutions.

India's trade expansion could add $140 billion to its economy by 2035, reshaping global markets and raising new challenges for U.S. agriculture.
On October 12, 2026, Bloomberg Economics published an analysis projecting that India's expanding free trade agreements could add $140 billion to its economy by 2035, potentially reshaping international commerce as countries respond to higher U.S. tariffs and diversify their trading relationships. The findings matter for American agriculture because changes in preferential market access could influence commodity competition, agricultural exports and supply chains, creating both opportunities and risks for U.S. farmers, cooperatives and agribusiness companies.
The projections come as India accelerates trade negotiations with major economic partners, including the European Union, while strengthening commercial relationships across Asia and the Middle East. According to Bloomberg Economics economists Eleonora Mavroeidi, Abhishek Gupta and Maeva Cousin, agreements already implemented could lift India's GDP by 1.2% by 2035 compared with a baseline without those deals. The estimated gain increases to 1.7%, or approximately $140 billion, if additional agreements with the European Union and New Zealand are implemented as modeled.
The broader implications extend beyond India's domestic economic performance. Bloomberg Economics estimates that additional agreements involving other trading partners could raise the country's GDP gain to 2.1%, equivalent to approximately $170 billion by 2035. Under a scenario in which all modeled agreements are implemented, Indian exports could increase by nearly 10% compared with the baseline. For U.S. agriculture, the significance lies in the potential redistribution of trade flows, investment and commercial relationships across global markets, rather than in any guaranteed increase in agricultural imports.
How India's Trade Strategy Could Change U.S. Agricultural Competitiveness
India's commercial expansion is unfolding against a backdrop of significant changes in U.S. trade policy. Bloomberg Economics estimates that the average U.S. tariff rate reached 10.7% in August 2026, compared with 2.3% in 2024, increasing pressure on international trading relationships. The researchers project that tariffs at those levels could reduce overall U.S. merchandise imports by approximately 15% compared with the previous regime. As trading partners seek alternative markets, preferential agreements could increasingly influence where companies invest and source products.
For American farmers and agricultural exporters, the competitive consequences will depend on the specific products covered by trade agreements. Soybeans, cotton, tree nuts, pulses and other agricultural commodities may face different market conditions depending on tariffs, import regulations and competition from alternative suppliers. However, the Bloomberg Economics analysis does not provide commodity-specific forecasts for U.S. agriculture. Any assessment of individual crops must therefore consider USDA trade statistics, existing import restrictions and the final provisions of future bilateral agreements.
India's agricultural market presents particular complexities because trade liberalization does not necessarily mean unrestricted access for foreign farm products. In its modeling, Bloomberg Economics assumes that India eliminates tariffs on industrial products while reducing agricultural tariffs by half over a ten-year implementation period. This is a modeling assumption, not a confirmed schedule for every agreement. Actual agricultural market access will depend on negotiated tariff lines, exclusions, quotas and sanitary requirements, all of which can materially affect U.S. export competitiveness.
The potential implications also extend to agricultural cooperatives, food processors and international commodity traders. Companies managing global sourcing strategies may need to reassess purchasing relationships as tariff preferences and logistics costs evolve. Lower trade barriers can create opportunities for agricultural exporters, but they can also strengthen competing suppliers. For U.S. producers facing volatile commodity prices, elevated input costs and uncertainty over international demand, understanding these developments will be important for marketing decisions and long-term investment planning.
India's Agricultural Transformation Opens Opportunities and Risks for American Agribusiness
One of the most consequential aspects of India's economic outlook involves its agricultural workforce. The Bloomberg Economics report notes that more than 40% of Indian workers remain employed in agriculture, reflecting a substantial concentration of labor in a sector characterized by underemployment and relatively low productivity. The researchers examine a scenario in which improved farm productivity enables workers to transition into manufacturing and services. Under those assumptions, structural changes could add approximately two percentage points to India's projected GDP gains by 2035.
The analysis compares India's development trajectory with Vietnam, where agriculture's share of total employment has declined significantly as industrial activity expanded. Bloomberg Economics reports that agricultural output per worker in Vietnam now exceeds India's by almost 60%, illustrating the potential economic impact of productivity improvements. For agricultural technology providers, India's modernization needs could create commercial opportunities in mechanization, irrigation systems, precision agriculture, digital farm management and agricultural infrastructure, although these opportunities are not quantified in the report.
American agricultural equipment manufacturers, technology developers and agribusiness investors may find India's productivity challenge strategically relevant. Expanding farm efficiency often requires machinery, improved logistics, better resource management and access to modern production technologies. Precision agriculture, sustainable agriculture practices and supply chain modernization could become increasingly important as India's economy develops. Nevertheless, commercial opportunities will depend on domestic policies, investment conditions, local competition and the ability of foreign companies to enter the market.
The U.S.-India trade relationship remains another important variable. Bloomberg Economics estimates that the average tariff applied to Indian goods entering the United States increased from 2.4% in 2024 to 11.6% in August 2026. Its model suggests these higher duties could reduce India's merchandise exports to the U.S. market by roughly one-fifth by 2035. However, the projected impact on India's overall GDP is limited because the economy could partially offset reduced American demand through stronger exports to other destinations.
For Washington, these developments raise questions about how future trade negotiations could support agricultural market access while addressing domestic economic priorities. U.S. farm policy, including the farm bill, crop insurance programs and USDA export promotion initiatives, operates alongside trade policy in shaping the industry's competitive environment. Although Bloomberg's projections do not assess those programs directly, their interaction with commodity prices, production costs and international demand will remain relevant for producers evaluating long-term financial and operational risks.
The central distinction is that India's projected $140 billion economic gain is not a forecast of additional U.S. agricultural sales. It represents a modeled increase in India's economic output resulting from trade agreements, lower commercial barriers and associated investment effects. Agricultural benefits for American producers remain uncertain and will require more detailed analysis of individual markets. Still, the expansion of India's trade network illustrates how quickly global commercial relationships can evolve when major economies pursue new trading partners.
For U.S. farmers, agricultural cooperatives, exporters and policymakers, the emerging lesson is the importance of maintaining competitiveness in a more fragmented international marketplace. Market access, agricultural productivity, tariff policy and supply chain resilience will help determine how American agriculture responds to India's expanding economic influence. As negotiations advance, the industry's ability to identify new demand, manage trade risks and protect its position in global commodity markets could become increasingly important through 2035.

articles.title: IBM, MeitY Startup Hub partner to accelerate India’s deep-tech startup ecosystem - Express Computer

IBM and MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), an initiative of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to support deep-tech startups in India through access to enterprise technologies, technical mentorship, skilling programmes and commercialisation opportunities.
The collaboration will bring together MSH’s nationwide startup network and IBM’s expertise in artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid cloud and quantum computing. It aims to help startups build, validate and scale solutions for Indian and global markets, while creating opportunities to engage with enterprises, investors and industry experts.
The agreement also complements IBM Ventures’ existing engagements in India, extending support for enterprise technology startups through IBM’s technology portfolio and industry ecosystem.
Dr Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO of MeitY Startup Hub, said the partnership would support the development of indigenous deep-tech capabilities and technology-led entrepreneurship.
“India’s startup ecosystem is emerging as a global engine for technology innovation. Through this collaboration with IBM, we aim to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities, foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat,” he said.
Access to enterprise AI, cloud and quantum technologies
Under the MoU, startups will gain access to IBM’s enterprise technology portfolio and innovation platforms to develop solutions for business use cases. These include technical guidance on IBM watsonx, its enterprise AI and data platform; IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises; and IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty.
The programme will also offer technical orientation on hybrid cloud and quantum computing, alongside access to security and automation solutions.
IBM and MSH will jointly explore initiatives for startups at different stages of growth, with potential applications across banking and financial services, government and industrial sectors. The focus areas include enterprise proof-of-concept projects, sovereign AI innovation, open-source ecosystem development, founder mentorship and technical skilling.
The partners also plan to create opportunities for startups to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors. A key priority is to identify and nurture innovators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, broadening access to the country’s deep-tech ecosystem.
Focus on scaling innovation and commercialisation
Sandip Patel, managing director, IBM India and South Asia, said the collaboration would help startups develop solutions addressing challenges in India and international markets.
“These startups are playing a pivotal role in shaping the future of technology-led growth for India and the world,” Patel said. “Together with MeitY Startup Hub, we aim to help founders innovate faster, scale responsibly, and build solutions that address both national and global challenges – turning promising innovation into real-world impact.”
The partnership builds on IBM’s work with startups, developers, academic institutions and ecosystem partners in India, including initiatives focused on technology access, technical mentorship and skills development.
IBM Ventures supports founders building enterprise technology companies through a capital-plus model, combining investment with access to IBM’s global reach, technology expertise and network of specialists to help startups scale.
The MoU adds another channel for connecting India’s deep-tech founders with enterprise requirements and potential routes to commercialisation. While the announcement outlines the areas of collaboration, it does not specify funding commitments, the number of startups to be supported or a timeline for individual programmes.

Tata Sons chairman says long-term bets must be judged beyond immediate returns, while stressing the need to balance growth ambitions with financial viability, demand and execution.
Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran on Tuesday defended the Tata Group’s long-term investment strategy amid a boardroom tussle over capital allocation, saying projects critical to India’s future cannot be judged solely by the returns they generate over the next two to three years.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Chandrasekaran said the group would continue building businesses and capabilities that India and the world need, including semiconductor manufacturing, even when such investments take time to deliver results.
“Direction is certain, need is certain, ability to execute is certain,” he said, while cautioning that investment decisions must be guided by demand and financial viability. “We can’t be reckless,” he added.
His remarks come amid differences between Chandrasekaran and Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata over capital allocation and the pace at which investments should generate returns. Tata Trusts owns about 66% of Tata Sons, the holding company of the nearly 160-year-old conglomerate.
The disagreement has come into sharper focus following the Tata Sons board’s decision in September to reappoint Chandrasekaran for a five-year term, despite his earlier indication that he would not seek another term when his existing tenure ends in February 2027.
Noel Tata, one of the two Tata Trusts nominees on the Tata Sons board, voted against the reappointment. Tata Trusts subsequently questioned its legality, citing a legal opinion, while Tata Sons has disputed that position, setting the stage for a potential legal battle over the group’s leadership.
Chandrasekaran’s comments underline the competing considerations confronting the conglomerate: investing for long-term growth while maintaining financial discipline and meeting shareholder expectations on returns.
He said the past decisions had been vindicated over the long term, adding that businesses must correct course when things go wrong. He also stressed the importance of monitoring the balance sheet and assessing demand before committing capital.
“You need to feel the stones and cross the river. It is not that you are going to have a very clean spreadsheet in this uncertain world,” he said, describing the challenges of evaluating investments amid uncertainty.
The Tata Group’s semiconductor plans are among its major long-term bets. Tata Electronics is setting up a fabrication plant at Dholera in Gujarat with an investment of around ₹91,000 crore, in partnership with Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation. It is also developing an assembly and testing facility in Assam involving around ₹27,000 crore.
Chandrasekaran said semiconductors would be fundamental to India’s future, citing the country’s talent pool, domestic market and potential to participate in global supply chains. However, he cautioned against pursuing advanced chipmaking technologies without adequate demand or a commercially viable business case.
The broader challenge, his remarks suggest, is to balance the group’s ambitions in strategic industries with the need for sustainable returns and disciplined capital allocation.

Dr. Sunil K. articles.title: IMF raises India’s 2026 growth forecast to 7%, up from 6.4% - Mangalore Today
articles.summary: IMF raises India’s 2026 growth forecast to 7%, up from 6.4%  Mangalore Today
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct 13, 2026: India’s economy is projected to grow 7% in the year 2026, up from the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) earlier estimate of 6.4%, as resilient domestic demand and strong services activity continue to support growth despite elevated oil prices and geopolitical uncertainties.
In its October World Economic Outlook (WEO), the IMF also raised India’s growth forecast for 2027  to 7% from 6.7% projected earlier, signalling that the country’s economic momentum could remain strong over the next two financial years.
The upward revision follows stronger-than-expected economic performance in the first quarter of FY27, when India’s gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.8% year-on-year. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has also raised its GDP growth forecast for FY27 to 7.1% from 6.7% earlier.
India continues to stand out among major economies at a time when the global growth outlook remains uneven, with rising energy costs, geopolitical tensions and trade-related uncertainties weighing on several countries.
Why IMF Has Raised India’s Growth Forecast
The IMF attributed the improved outlook to resilient domestic demand and robust services activity, which have helped India sustain economic expansion despite higher energy costs and disruptions in the global economy.
Favourable demographic trends, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms are also expected to support India’s medium-term growth potential.
The latest revision reflects the stronger-than-anticipated performance of the Indian economy and follows upward adjustments to growth projections by other institutions.
According to the IMF’s projections, India’s economy expanded 7.8% in FY26. Growth is expected to moderate to 7% in FY27 before remaining at the same level in FY28.
However, higher crude oil prices remain a key risk for the economy, given India’s dependence on imported energy. A sustained increase in oil prices could push up domestic inflation, widen the current account deficit and increase pressure on the rupee.
IMF Global Growth Outlook: World Economy To Grow 3.1% In 2026
The IMF expects global economic growth to slow from 3.5% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026, before improving to 3.4% in 2027.
IMF said, “The global economy remains resilient, but that resilience is becoming more fragile and more uneven. Growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, while inflation is expected to reach 4.7%, driven largely by higher energy and food prices."
The outlook highlights diverging growth trajectories across economies, depending on their exposure to higher energy prices and their ability to benefit from the global technology upturn.
China’s economic growth is projected to slow to 4.5% in 2026 from 5% in 2025, before easing further to 4% in 2027. Higher oil prices, weak domestic demand and persistent structural challenges are expected to weigh on the Chinese economy.
The relative resilience of India’s growth outlook is particularly notable as several emerging economies that depend heavily on energy imports face pressure from rising commodity prices.
The IMF has warned that further disruptions to oil supplies, renewed trade tensions and tighter financial conditions could pose risks to the global economic outlook.
Inflation To Rise To 5% In FY27: IMF
Despite the stronger growth outlook, the IMF expects inflationary pressures in India to increase during the current financial year.
India’s consumer price inflation is projected to average 5% in FY27, compared with 2% in FY26, before easing to 4.4% in FY28.
The IMF’s FY27 inflation forecast is slightly below the RBI’s estimate of 5.2%. Meanwhile, India’s retail inflation rose to 5.5% in September, its highest level under the new CPI series.
Higher energy and commodity prices could add to inflationary pressures, potentially complicating the RBI’s monetary policy decisions even as economic growth remains robust.
India’s Current Account Deficit May Widen
The IMF also expects India’s external balance to come under some pressure in 2026. India’s current account deficit is projected to widen to 1.5% of GDP in 2026 from 0.7% in 2025, before narrowing to 1.3% in 2027.
A higher import bill, particularly for crude oil, could contribute to the widening deficit if elevated energy prices persist. The impact on the external balance will also depend on export performance, services receipts and other foreign exchange inflows.
Overall, the IMF’s latest projections point to continued strength in India’s growth outlook, supported by domestic demand and services activity. However, rising inflation, higher oil prices and external vulnerabilities remain key factors to watch in the months ahead.

"Probably we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing the deal at the earliest possible time," Agrawal told reporters in New Delhi.
He said the signing would depend partly on the US formalising its overall tariff structure.

Asked whether the framework would take into account the US Trade Representative's Section 301 investigations into concerns related to excess capacity, Agrawal said, "I think all other issues will get settled as part of the deal".
Earlier this month, India and 14 other countries called for coordinated global action to curb excess industrial production that distorts markets, hurts domestic industries and contributes to an imbalance between supply and demand.

Agrawal said the range of outstanding issues had narrowed over time.
The framework for the first tranche of the India-US trade agreement was announced in February, but changes in the US tariff landscape led to further negotiations. India is seeking more favourable tariffs for its goods in the US market.

Context
Phased trade deals of this kind have followed a familiar sequence: a political announcement of agreement in principle, a legal drafting and scrubbing phase, a signing ceremony, and only later the published schedules that allow the tariff and market-access details to be priced properly. Headlines at the drafting stage have historically produced the smallest and least durable FX reaction, since nothing is yet enforceable and phases have been known to stall or be re-scoped before signature; the repricing, when it comes, tends to arrive with the text. The transmission channel here runs through India's tariff differential on US goods and any reciprocal concessions, which feeds INR primarily via expectations for trade balances and portfolio flows rather than through the broad dollar, so DXY relevance is limited. What separates a durable move from a fade is whether the first phase covers the contentious items, typically agriculture, digital trade and tariffs, or defers them to later phases, which has been the pattern in past bilateral deals structured this way. The follow-ons worth noting are the signing timeline, publication of the legal text, and any parallel statements from the US side, since divergent characterisations between negotiating parties have been a recurring feature of these processes. As a ministerial comment rather than a signed document, this is direction-setting rather than confirmation.

articles.title: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the context of increasingly fierce competition to attract foreign investment, India is linking incentives to revenue, domestic supply chains, and R&D activities. This approach is noteworthy as Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies to better align with project performance.
India is spending $7.5 billion, but not just to produce more phones.
On August 21, 2026, India announced the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme 2026 (MPMS), following the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme which ended on March 31.
During the four years of implementing the PLI (Private Partnership in the Mobile Industry), from 2022 to 2025, India's smartphone exports increased more than sevenfold, from $3.1 billion to $24.1 billion. By 2025, smartphones will become the country's largest export item. This result lays the foundation for India to move to the next phase in its mobile phone industry development strategy.
Instead of focusing solely on expanding manufacturing and assembly, India aims to become a global mobile phone manufacturing and export hub, while also integrating the domestic supply chain more deeply into the process. The MPMS (Mobile Manufacturing and Production Management System) is designed to link the growth of production and revenue for businesses with the use of domestically sourced components as well as design, research, and development (R&D) activities.
A notable aspect of MPMS is that support is determined based on the actual performance of the business. For large-scale manufacturers, the support amount is calculated based on the portion of revenue exceeding the standard revenue threshold. Businesses that reach a certain revenue threshold and continue to maintain growth will be eligible for support.
This mechanism also encourages businesses to increase their use of components sourced from the Indian market. Phones using domestically sourced components can receive an additional subsidy of up to 1.5%. These components include screens, cameras, phone casings, batteries, and charging cables.
Indian domestic brands are eligible for higher levels of support if they meet conditions regarding ownership structure, operational control, and intellectual property rights, while also establishing design and research centers within the country. Thus, the level of support depends not only on size and revenue growth but also on the extent of participation in the domestic supply chain, as well as design and R&D activities.
You may also like
To implement the MPMS, India has allocated 62,500 crore rupees, equivalent to approximately US$7.5 billion. The program spans five fiscal years, from 2026-2027 to 2030-2031, with grants determined based on business performance.
The design of the MPMS shows that India is not simply allocating resources to increase mobile phone production. By linking support levels to business results and specific business activities, the program simultaneously aims at three goals: expanding revenue, increasing the use of domestically sourced components, and bringing more design and R&D activities into India.
This also marks a shift after the PLI phase. While the previous phase contributed to the rapid expansion of smartphone production and exports, MPMS places greater emphasis on value creation and retention within the economy , through domestic supply chains and higher-tech activities.
What are the implications for Vietnam?
India's approach to linking support resources to business performance is particularly noteworthy in the context of increasing competition for investment among Asian economies, while Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies in line with Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy.
In a recent report, the Foreign Investment Agency of the Ministry of Finance noted that regional economies such as India, Malaysia , and Thailand are stepping up incentive packages to attract shifting capital flows, especially in strategic sectors like semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and renewable energy. This creates additional competitive pressure on Vietnam in attracting and retaining high-quality investment projects.
At the same time, the need to innovate the methods of investment incentives and support has been raised. Resolution 10 emphasizes the need to "gradually shift from traditional incentives to a support mechanism linked to the operational efficiency of projects."
You may also like
One of the tools Vietnam is using is the Investment Support Fund, established under Decree No. 182/2024/ND-CP. The fund aims to stabilize the investment environment; encourage and attract strategic investors and multinational corporations; and support domestic businesses in certain sectors requiring investment incentives. Businesses meeting the eligibility criteria can receive support for costs such as training, R&D, fixed asset investment, and the production of high-tech products.
The Investment Support Fund is designed for multiple sectors, rather than focusing on a specific industry like the MPMS. This difference highlights a noteworthy aspect of resource allocation. With the MPMS, India selects a specific industry, clearly defining desired outcomes, from revenue growth and domestic supply chain development to bringing design and R&D activities domestically, and then links support levels to each of those outcomes.
In the context of limited support resources and increasingly fierce competition for investment, the selection of priority sectors and the level of resource concentration have become crucial factors in policy design and implementation. Focusing more on a few industries and sectors with the potential to create high added value, form supply chains, and disseminate technology can help support resources have a more significant impact, rather than allocating them too broadly.
Besides leveraging the effectiveness of the Investment Support Fund under Decree 182 to retain investors and supply chains, in the face of fierce competition to attract investment, India's method of quantifying results to determine the level of support in the MPMS program provides valuable experience for Vietnam as it gradually shifts from traditional incentives to performance-based support mechanisms in the future.

Sri Lanka must widen its tax net rather than place an ever-greater burden on the existing taxpayers, CA Sri Lanka said, urging the government to use Budget 2027 to turn the economic stability into stronger growth.
With the national budget due on November 12, CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe called for a broader, fairer and more sustainable revenue system, supported by greater formalisation, stronger compliance and digitalisation.
“Our Budget 2027 proposals focused on a fundamental question: how do we build a revenue system that is broader, fairer and more sustainable, without placing an ever-greater burden on those already within the tax net?” he said addressing the 47th National Conference of CA Sri Lanka.
“We need a broader tax base, greater formalisation, better compliance, digitalisation and a tax system that people regard as fair.”
Subasinghe stressed that fiscal policy must also support the country’s transition from stabilisation to growth, with the forthcoming budget assuming particular importance.
“The government, business and professions must continue to listen to one another. Because ultimately, a country cannot tax its way to prosperity. We must grow our way to prosperity.”
Among CA Sri Lanka’s proposals was an increase in the monthly Advance Personal Income Tax threshold to Rs.200,000, providing relief to the middle-income earners while recognising the fiscal implications of the measure.
Subasinghe welcomed the government’s subsequent indication that it remained committed to moving the personal income-tax-free threshold towards Rs.200,000, although he said it remained a “wait and see situation”. He said the professional institutions had a responsibility to contribute constructively to policy formulation, rather than merely comment on decisions.
The tax proposals formed part of a broader argument that Sri Lanka’s recovery must now generate the investment, employment, productivity and foreign exchange needed to sustain its economic gains.
“Therefore, our challenge is not simply to avoid another default. It is to build an economy capable of generating sufficient growth, exports, investment and revenue to service our obligations while improving the quality of life of our people,” Subasinghe said.
He called for growth that creates jobs, allows businesses to invest and expand, raises productivity and brings more people into the formal economy.
Reflecting on the recovery, Subasinghe said Sri Lanka had recorded 11 consecutive quarters of economic growth, while the gross official reserves had risen to US $ 6.9 billion.
The reserves had stood at US $ 7.3 billion in February before absorbing the subsequent oil-price shocks, highlighting the continuing need to strengthen the country’s external buffers.
That position contrasted sharply with the crisis four years earlier, when inflation had approached 70 percent and the gross official reserves had fallen to around US $ 1.9 billion. According to Subasinghe, about US $ 1.5 billion of that amount was held under the People’s Bank of China swap arrangement, leaving less than US $ 400 million in immediately usable reserves.
“For a nation that needed to pay for fuel, food, medicine and essential imports, this was not simply an economic crisis. It was a fight for basic survival.”
However, he cautioned against treating stabilisation as the end of the recovery process.
“The next phase of our national journey must be about more than recovering from the crisis and stability. Now it must be about growth and resilience,” he said, questioning whether the country had the right policies to accelerate growth.
Subasinghe acknowledged the International Monetary Fund (IMF)-supported Extended Fund Facility’s role in restoring fiscal discipline, rebuilding reserves, advancing debt restructuring and strengthening confidence since 2023.
With the programme approaching its conclusion and its final review scheduled for 2027, he identified three possible paths for Sri Lanka: another IMF programme, a home-grown programme or a hybrid of the two.
Whether to enter another programme was a decision for the government, he said. However, the principles underpinning the recovery needed to become part of the country’s economic culture.
“Above all, we must ensure that the reforms we undertake are not reforms we implement because someone is watching us but reforms we uphold because we have learnt their value.”
Subasinghe also warned that the relief secured through debt restructuring did not remove the need to strengthen Sri Lanka’s capacity to meet its obligations.
He credited the current and previous governments for the restructuring effort, which he said had delivered substantial relief, including a targeted reduction of around US $ 17 billion in external debt service during the IMF programme period.
“Debt relief is not the same as debt elimination. The debt remains.”
He stressed that Sri Lanka needed additional foreign exchange and stronger reserves to meet its debt commitments while retaining the capacity to absorb the external shocks.
The debt sustainability framework also constrained the fiscal space available to the policymakers, he said, citing targets to bring public debt below 95 percent of GDP by 2032, keep average annual gross financing needs below 13 percent of GDP during 2027-2032 and annual foreign-currency debt service below 4.5 percent of GDP over the same period.
“These are not merely numbers in an IMF document. They are a reminder of the fiscal space we must protect.”
The geopolitical tensions added to those challenges, with Subasinghe warning that the conflict in the Middle East could affect the fuel prices, port-related transport costs, tourism and migrant earnings, ultimately influencing the foreign exchange available for debt service.
The shifting supply chains, risks to shipping routes and vulnerable energy markets meant Sri Lanka’s next phase of growth needed to build resilience alongside the competitiveness.
He urged the country to aspire to an economy that generates its own foreign exchange and attracts investment, technology, knowledge and talent, while offering young people stronger reasons to build their futures at home.
