The New Yalu River Bridge, which spans 3 kilometres across the Yalu River, officially opened to traffic on Thursday. This new infrastructure connects the Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), marking a significant moment in the bilateral relations between these neighbouring countries.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the bridge as 'an important facility for connectivity' that would enhance trade and exchanges between the two nations. The opening ceremony signifies a warming trend in economic ties, which had been considerably affected by political tensions in previous years.
Originally slated for completion in 2014, the bridge faced delays primarily due to North Korea's cessation of construction on its side of the border. The New Yalu River Bridge serves as a modern alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built during the Japanese occupation of the Korean Peninsula between 1937 and 1943.
The bridge is expected to play a crucial role in increasing the volume of trade, which last year saw a recovery to $2.7 billion, largely driven by Chinese exports to North Korea. However, experts caution that a significant surge in trade is unlikely, given ongoing United Nations sanctions against North Korea. According to Kang Jun-young, a professor focusing on Chinese studies, North Korea remains wary of excessive Chinese imports that could diminish its sovereignty in the domestic market.
China has historically been North Korea's primary trading partner, and the relationship is underscored by a mutual defence treaty. The alliance, described as 'close as lips and teeth' by former Chinese leader Mao Zedong, has experienced fluctuations, particularly due to North Korea's nuclear ambitions. There have been signs of renewed cooperation, particularly following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Pyongyang in June 2026.
The New Yalu River Bridge is seen as a symbol of improving ties. It comes at a time when North Korea has been strengthening its relationship with Russia, notably amidst the geopolitical changes following the Ukraine conflict, which may further influence its economic and diplomatic strategies.
The successful opening of the bridge reflects efforts by both countries to enhance their strategic partnership while navigating the complexities imposed by international sanctions and regional security dynamics.

articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Krishna Srinivasan, Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, was asked how India should read the gap between strong domestic growth and pressure from external markets, and what it would take for growth to stay resilient. "India entered this with very strong fundamentals," he said.
Also read: Asia set to ‘continue to outpace the world’, says IMF, as it asks central banks to stay focused on price stability
Growth was strong and fiscal prudence was firmly in place, he said, and "they have responded well to the shock".
The rupee has risen for four straight sessions, according to PTI, after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced a set of measures on October 10 to stem its fall.
Exchange rate not a sign of failure
The World Economic Outlook describes the wider backdrop. It said benchmark interest rates in advanced economies have climbed to multi-decade highs, pushing up borrowing costs for emerging markets. Exchange rates have been highly volatile, especially in Asia, it said.
The IMF's baseline assumes oil at about $96 a barrel in 2026, and that the Strait of Hormuz reopens from March 2027.
RBI steps in, rupee gains
The RBI opened a special window on October 10 to meet the entire daily dollar needs of three state-run oil marketing companies, Indian Oil, Hindustan Petroleum and Bharat Petroleum, according to PTI. The window started on October 12 and will stay in place until further notice. It takes their dollar demand out of the spot market.
The central bank also tightened rules on forex derivatives to curb speculative bets against the rupee. Authorised dealers cannot allow users to rebook any rupee forex derivative contract that has been cancelled, PTI reported. Banks must also hold a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve equal to 20 per cent of the notional amount of each eligible contract above $2 million. The reserve applies to contracts hedging current account transactions where the user is buying foreign currency against the rupee.
The rupee closed at 95.17 against the dollar on Wednesday, its fourth straight session of gains and a one-month high, according to PTI. It rose 171 paise over the four sessions, and forex traders told PTI the rise reflected the RBI's measures.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Tuesday that the rupee has depreciated "significantly" over the past year and a half and that the RBI will continue efforts to prevent excessive volatility, PTI reported. She said most of the volatility comes from external challenges, while the government keeps domestic fundamentals sound.
In its October 7 policy statement, the RBI said it is committed to "orderly adjustments to the exchange rate" in line with macroeconomic fundamentals and to curbing excessive volatility. It said India's forex reserves stood at $734.6 billion as of October 2, enough for about 11 months of imports. The central bank also said foreign portfolio investors pulled out a net $10.3 billion between April and October 5, while net foreign direct investment rose to $13.8 billion in April-August. On the same day it raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent.
Growth revised up on a strong first quarter
Srinivasan said the IMF raised its India growth forecast because the April-June quarter came in much stronger than it had expected. The Fund now sees growth at 7 per cent this year and next, he said, and 6.9 per cent over the medium term.
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) put real GDP growth at 7.8 per cent for April-June.
The Fund's World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, shows India at 7.0 per cent in both 2026-27 and 2027-28. On a calendar-year basis the figures are 7.4 per cent for 2026 and 7.0 per cent for 2027. The 2026 forecast is 0.5 percentage point higher than in April and 0.6 point higher than in July.
The report said India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, backed by resilient domestic demand and strong services activity.
It also said India stands out in the medium-term outlook with upward revisions. It credited favourable demographics, a large and growing domestic market and continued structural reforms. Among major economies, India is an exception in not needing more fiscal consolidation than currently planned to keep its debt ratio at 2025 levels, the report said.
IMF on India's GDP data revisions
Srinivasan was also asked about the revisions to India's GDP numbers. He said the authorities have issued a note explaining the revisions, and that the changes in methodology are "entirely consistent" with the advice the IMF has given, including from its statistics department. What MoSPI has done is in line with good practice, he said.
"There's always room for improvement," Srinivasan said, but the good work done by MoSPI in improving GDP statistics should be recognised.
MoSPI released a new GDP series with 2022-23 as the base year, replacing 2011-12, on February 27 this year. The ministry said the quarterly estimates follow guidelines in the IMF's Quarterly National Accounts Manual of 2017.
Asia's wider picture
In his opening remarks, Srinivasan said Asia's growth is projected to ease from 5 per cent in 2025 to 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 4.4 per cent in 2027, still ahead of the world. "Growth has surprised on the upside in India," he said, while countries that do not gain directly from the technology boom have seen their forecasts cut.
Also read: IMF sees India bucking global slowdown, raises 2026 growth forecast to 7%
He said risks remain tilted to the downside, including prolonged or renewed tension in the Middle East and an El Nino that could add to fiscal and inflation pressure. Support for people hit by the shocks should be targeted, he said, with the idea being to "protect people and not prices".
He named four reform priorities for the region. These are tackling youth unemployment and skill gaps while helping workers adapt to AI, strengthening social protection, improving energy security, and deepening regional integration.
